#5721. XPENG Sales Soar!

XPENG had a fantabulous sales month in October. We can give you the numbers, but as you can see well enough in the chart above and below, the company’s sales soared to a whole new level last month.

Reaching 50,237 vehicle deliveries, that meant 22% sales growth month over month and 20% sales growth year over year. Will it be another year until XPENG beats its monthly sales record again, or is the October 2026 result just the beginning of more record sales in coming months?

Well, there are some reasons to expect even more growth. “In October 2026, the XPENG L05 was officially launched in the Chinese mainland, with deliveries set to begin on November 1, 2026,” XPENG shares. “On October 26, 2026, XPENG obtained a demonstration operation license to conduct Level 4 Robotaxi services in Guangzhou. #5720. 1976 Pontiac Trans Am For Sale With 7 Miles After Restoration Pairs 4-Speed Stick And 455 V8

For those looking to channel your inner Burt Reynolds from "Smokey and the Bandit," WeBe Autos (via Hemmings) has this lovely black-and-gold Trans Am for sale that's nearly the perfect match. Except, it's a 1976, not a 1978, so it doesn't feature the quad-headlight front-end that the movie car had. If that's what you want, however, this 1978 example or this 1979 one that's done roughly 22,000 miles should be of interest. Neither of them, mind you, is in black, nor do they feature a 455-cubic-inch V8 or offer the three-pedal experience like the '76 example we have here.

Unlike the movie car, though, this Trans Am is a hardtop coupé. But it has undergone extensive restoration and has only done seven miles since. And yes, it has the Screaming Chicken hood decal, or the "Rising Phoenix" if you're part of that camp. So what's the asking price for this 1970s muscle-car goodness? That'd be $72,495. Although it may not be as sophisticated as the latest BMW iX3 (also a $70,000 ballpark proposition), the 455 V8 and four-speed combo has enough personality and aura to challenge whatever these modern-day "computers on wheels" can offer.

Character assessment aside, what you get for your money is a well-finished exterior, a beautifully detailed engine compartment, an exceptionally clean underbody, and a beautifully restored all-black interior. While the Endura-style bumpers and Honeycomb wheels stand out as exterior highlights, the classic Trans Am instrumentation, custom Autosound audio system, and factory-style dashboard come across as some of the notable attractions on the inside. Sure, it might not be a T-top nor feature the movie car's front fascia, but then again, Bandit's companion was actually a 1976 Trans Am with a '77 front end.

Classic Industries and Hemmings reckon there were four cars used in total, while Autoweek counts five, but the important thing is that all Trans Ams used in the movie started out as '76 Special Edition 50th Anniversary cars with the updated '77 front end. Pontiac had to get creative because the movie's production began before 1977 models were actually available. And the engines you saw (or rather heard) on screen weren't part of the 1977 lineup at all. While Classic Industries reported the stunt cars retaining the 455 V8, in reality, you could not have optioned the motor in a 1977 car — it was retired after the 1976 model year.

Setting aside this bit of "Smokey and the Bandit" trivia, you can probably already tell how the Trans Am listing we have ties in with all this. It's a 1976 car in the right paint scheme, with the 455 and a four-speed manual thrown in for good measure. More importantly, there's no deception here, and it looks nothing like a 50-year-old hunk of metal.

Is the near-$73,000 asking price too much? That depends on whom you ask. It's a lot of money for something that old. Despite the restoration, that 455 was part of the Malaise Era lineup, which famously neutered a lot of high-performance V8s. Given that the listing mentions "emissions equipment present," it's unlikely that things are any different here. Still, for someone who likes '70s Americana, is an ardent fan of movies, or, above all, a true-blue Pontiac enthusiast, this Trans Am should hold plenty of appeal. Assuming, of course, they have the means to afford it.

#5719. Shorter Days and Dark Afternoons Can Trigger Depression

— Scientists are trying to understand what causes SAD

As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there's also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.

In 1984, a team led by Norman Rosenthal, MD, then a researcher at the NIH, first described SAD and coined the term. "I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck," he said.

Scientists Are Trying to Understand What Causes SAD

No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.

In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.

Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains' alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.

Researcher Kathryn Roecklein, PhD, at the University of Pittsburgh, tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.

When Days Get Shorter, Powerful Light Can Help

Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Paul Desan, MD, PhD, of Yale University's Winter Depression Research Clinic in New Haven, Connecticut. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.

Research supports using a light that's about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.

Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.

Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.

If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.

Talk Therapy and Medication Can Also Help Some With SAD

Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.

Light therapy's benefits can fade when people stop using it. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, said Kelly Rohan, PhD, of the University of Vermont in Burlington.

Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Those with SAD should try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.

Ferrari made the announcement that its first all-electric vehicle was sold out through '27 during its earnings call earlier this week, according to InsideEVs. #5714. Pascal Tricuspid TEER Handed Soft Victory in 'Hamstrung' CLASP II TR Trial

— Pascal Precision device was recently approved by the FDA

The Pascal Precision transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) system eked out a win in symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) in its pivotal randomized trial.

In CLASP II TR, there was significant clinical improvement among patients randomized to tricuspid valve TEER plus optimal medical therapy, as opposed to medical therapy alone, in a hierarchical analysis counting all-cause death, right ventricular assist device implantation or heart transplant, tricuspid valve intervention, number of heart failure (HF) hospitalizations, and overall health status.

This primary endpoint produced a win ratio of 1.98 favoring the Pascal Precision (95% CI 1.47-2.67), reported Charles Davidson, MD, of Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics (TCT) annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

The TEER benefit was driven by 6-month health status improvement alone: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores were on average over 10 points higher in the device group compared with controls, according to co-trialist Suzanne Arnold, MD, MHA, of Saint Luke's Mid America Heart Institute in Kansas City, Missouri, speaking alongside Davidson.

"The CLASP II TR trial demonstrates safety and efficacy of the Pascal system to improve health status in symptomatic patients with [severe or greater] TR," the study authors concluded.

The efficacy results were not what the authors had originally hoped for, however, as CLASP II TR was initially designed for a 24-month primary endpoint -- only later revised to 6 months due to control group attrition to commercial therapy following FDA approval of the Evoque tricuspid valve replacement system and the TriClip G4 TEER device in 2024.

Still, it was on the basis of this study that the Pascal Precision recently got FDA approval for tricuspid valve repair. Initially, the device had entered the market for mitral TEER in 2022.

Co-investigator and TCT panelist Rebecca Hahn, MD, of NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, maintained that despite the "hamstrung" analyses in CLASP II TR, "it does in the end add to the literature supporting the treatment of these patients with [tricuspid] TEER."

Indeed, CLASP II TR marks the fourth trial (after TRILUMINATE, Tri.Fr, and TRIC-I-HF) to show superiority of tricuspid valve repair over medical therapy, especially concerning patient-reported outcomes, noted Jörg Hausleiter, MD, of Klinikum Der Universitat Munchen in Germany, the study discussant at TCT.

In fact, Hausleiter's TRIC-I-HF study had the distinction of being the landmark study showing that, among the selected population of sicker people with severe TR at high risk for future HF events, transcatheter tricuspid intervention reduced all-cause death and HF hospitalization while improving quality of life.

Davidson and Arnold reported that their trial was also able to give tricuspid TEER the edge for proportion of patients alive with ≥20-point improvements in the KCCQ overall score at 6 months (38.8% vs 12.3%, P<0.001), as well as the proportion alive with more modest ≥10-point improvements in KCCQ (57.1% vs 25.4%, P<0.001). Additionally, those achieving moderate or better TR at 1 year came out to 80% with the device versus 30% with only medical therapy.

For the TEER recipients, the composite safety event rate reached 6.9% at 30 days and 20.1% at 1 year. Among the most frequent events were single leaflet device attachment (3.4% and 4.8%, respectively), severe bleeding (3.1% and 8.5%), and cardiovascular mortality (0.3% and 5.4%).

"I think it's important to help people feel better," said Patrick O'Gara, MD, of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, also a panelist at TCT. "If patients are feeling better, it's a good outcome provided the procedure is safe and is provided by people who are expert in its implementation."

"In some ways, we should be cautious, we need to temper expectations ... There are huge gaps between expectations and the reality of what we're able to achieve," O'Gara told the audience.

The CLASP II TR trial, conducted in the U.S. and Canada, had participants with severe-or-worse TR randomized to Pascal Precision TEER with medical therapy (n=294) or medical therapy alone (n=148).

The cohort averaged about 80 years old, with just under half being women. Nearly 60% had New York Heart Association class III-IV symptoms. STS-PROM (for mitral valve repair) scores were about 7.5%. Approximately one in four people had a HF hospitalization in the past 12 months.

TR etiology was largely secondary (over 75%) and most commonly graded as severe (58%) as opposed to massive or torrential.

The authors reported that 92.5% of the treatment arm got the device implanted successfully. This group was roughly split between those who got one and two devices.

Davidson and Arnold noted that their open-label trial left room for a placebo effect. Participating centers and operators also generally had limited prior experience with the Pascal system, they added.

One important remaining question is when operators should intervene on TR.

During a press conference, Roxana Mehran, MD, of Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City, stressed the importance of the heart team and the fact that in the U.S., tricuspid TEER is still covered with evidence development. The expectation is that TVT registry data will continue to accrue to show who is the right patient at the right time for tricuspid TEER, she suggested.

The TVT registry has the downside of being single-arm, Arnold noted, but she agreed that it will still be helpful for providing long-term data.

#5713. Scandal-Ridden Cadillac F1 Owner Putting Team Up For Sale After Just One Year

The long-awaited entry of an American factory team was viewed as a coup for Formula 1. Billionaire financier Mark Walter is now looking to sell the Cadillac F1 Team after a single F1 season. While the team has failed to score a point in its maiden campaign so far, the sale would help him dodge scrutiny amid federal investigations into alleged self-dealing. Walter's TWG Group is in negotiations to sell a significant team stake at a $3 billion valuation.

Walter amassed a sports empire over the past 15 years. His investment firm Guggenheim Partners purchased the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2012 for $2.15 billion. Walter personally owns 27% of the MLB franchise. Since the acquisition, the Dodgers have alarmingly amassed over $1 billion in deferred payroll obligations on their way to three World Series titles. TWG would expand into racing in 2024, purchasing Andretti Global and its F1 entry bid. The company spent over $1 billion on the Cadillac F1 Team before its debut race in Australia earlier this year, nearly half that total was an anti-dilution fee.

How could Walter afford to do all of this? According to The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating how TWG-owned insurance companies lent billions of dollars to Walter's other enterprises. IndyCar fans are familiar with these insurance companies, seeing Delaware Life and Gainbridge logos plastered on Andretti's cars. An internal review found that $20 billion in loans weren't disclosed to financial regulators. Walter presumably needs to repay said $20 billion as soon as possible.

The TWG firesale began in August. Walter sold the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion to Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital. The deal was negotiated over a weekend. He added the NBA team to his sports empire just last year for $10 billion. After the Lakers deal, TWG denied that the Cadillac F1 Team was for sale. Despite the denial, Fenway Sports Group is the favorite among several bidders to buy the F1 team. The company currently owns the Boston Red Sox, Liverpool F.C. and RFK Racing in the NASCAR Cup Series.

The Cadillac F1 Team's sudden sale could be viewed as an opportunity for another automaker to enter Grand Prix racing, but General Motors also owns a stake in the team. With that constraint, FSG is the most logical choice to keep the team on its current course as GM develops its in-house F1 power unit program. Even without the federal investigations, Cadillac has had a rough start. The team has yet to score its first point. Team principal Graeme Lowdon was replaced in August. American F1 hopeful Colton Herta has yet to secure a Super License, partly due to the team misreporting Herta's past results to the FIA after believing an error on the IndyCar website.

#5711. “War” Secretary Pete Hegseth Endorses 15 Minute City Model

You just can’t make this stuff up. While conservatives around the world are waging holy war against the “15 Minute City” concept, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has gone all-in on the idea. His newly announced “Fortress America” military resilience plan includes a new vision for military bases that embraces walkability and quality of life. If that sounds like the 15 Minute City plan in action, it is. Oh, lordy…

Walkable communities are as old as the hills. That’s what people did before automobiles hit the scene and cities were organized around cars. Credit for applying the walkability model to 21st century urban planning goes to the Franco-Colombian scientist Carlos Moreno, who formalized the 15 Minute City concept in 2016. The idea got a further boost of attention when the Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, pitched walkable, bike-able neighborhoods as part of her successful re-election campaign in 2020.

The COVID-19 lockdown of 2020 was also a pivotal moment, with a surge in work-from-home households drawing attention to the need for local resources as a matter of survival and resiliency in case of a widespread emergency.

The 15 Minute City model covers a lot of ground, but the basic idea is that people should be able to do their shopping, recreation, socializing, and other essential routines within walking or biking distance from their homes, making cars largely optional within the neighborhood. Walkable access to schools and health care is also part of the plan.

The argument for 15-minute cities (also called 15-minute neighborhoods or 15-minute communities) is also pretty straightforward. Walking is healthier than sitting in a car. Avoiding injury or death from car accidents is another plus. Walking also reduces carbon emissions, and it saves money on gas.

In addition, walkability levels the playing field, so to speak. Everyone in the 15-minute zone has walkable access to basic resources, regardless of whether or not they can afford a car. In other words, there is a significant equity and inclusion element to the concept…

…and, that’s where the trouble kicks in. In 2022 the World Economic Forum posted an article by Lisa Chamberlain, the founder of the urban communications and business firm Strategies for City Builders. Chamberlain describes a 15 Minute City as characterized by diversified, mixed-use neighborhoods built to withstand shocks like COVID-19 and climate change.

“As climate change and global conflict cause shocks and stresses at faster intervals and increasing severity, the 15-minute city will become even more critical,” Chamberlain emphasized, with a further emphasis on equity and inclusion:

“Specifically, communities that foster and maintain social and economic relationships don’t have to be wealthy, but they do need to be walkable and safe, with both residential and commercial buildings intact. And, I would add, for 15-Minute Cities to thrive, not just survive crises—and this cannot be stressed enough—they must also have plenty of mixed-income and equitable housing, as well as digital access.”

It didn’t take long for the conspiracy machine to kick into action around the globe. In February of 2023, for example, the Australian news organization ABC radio summed up the 15 Minute City conspiracy theory thusly:

“To some, it’s an urban planning concept that promotes sustainable and healthy living.

“To a small group of others, it’s a plot by ‘tyrannical bureaucrats’ to take our cars and control our lives, which could lead to a real-life Hunger Games scenario.”

“Limiting cars and promoting pedestrian or bike access is framed as a slippery slope to government-run, open-air prisons,” ABC continued.

Yikes! ABC also cites the Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson. who railed against “idiot tyrannical bureaucrats” who “decide by fiat where you’re ‘allowed’ to drive…and, make no mistake, it’s part of a well-documented plan” (emphasis added).

Ohfergawdsakes, of course there is a well documented plan, and it’s called urban planning. And, that’s where the US Department of Defense comes in.

On September, in a move that sailed under the CleanTechnica radar, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the new “FORTRESS America” plan, with FORTRESS representing “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability.”

Stripping away Secretary Hegseth’s testosterone-fueled purple prose in the September 30 announcement, FORTRESS AMERICA applies the 15 Minute City urban planning model to major Defense Department bases in the US, ensuring they can operate independently of civilian infrastructure for a sustained period of time. That includes everything needed to support community life in addition to the supplies needed to sustain military operations.

FORTRESS America even goes beyond the initial 15 Minute City concept. As envisioned under the “Next Great American Base” element of the program, a central feature of the plan consists of access to a reliable source of on-site energy.

Don’t just take my word for it. “The program aligns basing and infrastructure projects to ensure they are collectively advancing toward greater independence,” Hegseth stated in the official order, with independence referring to the capability to sustain operations within a facility that is cut off from civilian resources. In other words, sustainable urban planning for military facilities.

Hegseth tasked the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment to carry out the new order. The base design part of the order was passed along to Dale Marks, the Assistant Secretary for Energy, Installations, and Environment.

Marks did not let the 15 Minute City grass grow under his feet. In a public presentation on October 29, he emphasized the importance of building quality of life into a sustainable model for military facilities in the US.

“Let us build installations worthy of the warriors who call them home,” Marks emphasized. “The nation shouldn’t expect warfighters to focus on high stakes, multidomain operations when they come home to base housing with black mold, failing plumbing and leaky roofs.”

“Substandard living conditions are not minor inconveniences. They are an active drain on morale, combat readiness and our retention of top-tier talent,” Marks elaborated.

It’s not just a matter of rehabbing military housing. In the presentation, Marks made the case for a full blown 15 Minute City model. “The Next Great American Base will include a compact, walkable concept with premier schools, advanced healthcare and town centers that foster community,” Marks continued, neatly summing up the fundamentals of 15 Minute Cities in a nutshell.

Marks anticipates that state governors and other stakeholders will compete to see where the first “Next Great American Base” will be constructed. Once complete, the new facility, and its 15 Minute City, will serve as a model for future projects.

As for the on-site power generation angle, nuclear energy gets the pole position — for now. As Marks and Hegseth both emphasize, though, speed is of the essence. Results are demanded within months, if not weeks. That leaves plenty of room for solar-enabled microgrids to throw their hat into the FORTRESS America ring. After all, if speed-to-power is the name, solar and batteries are the game…

Image: The 15 Minute City model calls for walkable, bike-able access to basic services and resources, a concept that has been embraced by none other than the US Department of Defense (courtesy of Rutgers University).

#5709. Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis

Scientists have identified hidden changes in the immune system that can appear up to 10 years before a person is diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The findings, presented at UEG Week 2026, suggest that certain antibody patterns in the blood could eventually help doctors identify people at risk of developing the condition and even predict how severe their disease might become.

Inflammatory bowel disease refers to a group of long-term disorders, including Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), that cause persistent inflammation in the digestive tract. These conditions develop when the immune system responds abnormally, contributing to inflammation and damage in the intestines.

Scientists increasingly believe that IBD begins developing years before it is officially diagnosed. However, the immune system changes that take place during this early, largely hidden period have remained poorly understood.

Tracking Immune Changes a Decade Before Diagnosis

To investigate what happens before IBD is diagnosed, researchers examined 2,000 blood serum samples collected from 500 people. The participants included 200 who eventually developed Crohn's disease, 200 who developed ulcerative colitis, and 100 healthy individuals of comparable age and sex.

Blood samples were available from the time of diagnosis and from approximately two, four, and 10 years earlier. This allowed the researchers to look backward through a decade of immune activity and identify changes that emerged before the diseases were recognized.

The team analyzed antibody reactions to approximately 357,000 antigens associated with bacteria, viruses, food, and the immune system itself. Antigens are substances that the immune system can recognize and respond to, while antibodies are proteins produced by the immune system that help identify specific targets.

Across all 2,000 samples, the researchers detected 123,980 unique antibodies.

A striking pattern emerged. People who later developed Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis had significantly less antibody diversity than healthy participants, meaning their immune systems showed a narrower range of antibody responses. Distinctive changes could be detected in both diseases as far back as 10 years before diagnosis.

Different Blood Signals Reveal Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis

The researchers also found that Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis were associated with different immune signatures.

Among people who later developed Crohn's disease, antibody responses to herpesviruses and bacterial flagellin were elevated. Flagellin is a protein that forms part of the tail-like structures some bacteria use to move.

These elevated responses were especially noticeable in individuals who eventually developed complicated Crohn's disease or disease affecting the ileum, the final section of the small intestine.

At the same time, antibody responses to encapsulated bacteria gradually decreased as diagnosis approached. These bacteria are surrounded by protective outer coatings that can help them evade immune defenses.

People who later developed ulcerative colitis showed a somewhat different pattern. Their antibody responses to herpesviruses and autoantigens increased, while responses to encapsulated pathogens declined. Autoantigens are components of the body's own tissues that can mistakenly become targets of an immune response.

Together, these findings suggest that the immune system undergoes measurable changes many years before inflammatory bowel disease is diagnosed.

AI Identifies Hidden Disease Risk Years in Advance

The researchers then used machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence that identifies patterns in complex data, to determine whether these antibody signatures could distinguish people who would eventually develop IBD from healthy individuals.

Using blood antibody patterns from up to 10 years before diagnosis, the models distinguished future Crohn's disease cases from healthy controls with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90. For ulcerative colitis, the corresponding value was 0.84.

AUC is a measure of how well a model distinguishes between two groups. A score of 0.5 indicates performance equivalent to chance, while 1.0 represents perfect discrimination.

The researchers also discovered that antibody patterns could help distinguish people who would develop complicated Crohn's disease from those whose disease would remain less complicated. This distinction was possible approximately 10 years before diagnosis, with an AUC of 0.85.

These findings raise the possibility that blood antibody testing could eventually help identify not only who is at increased risk of IBD, but also which patients may need more intensive treatment.

Commenting on the findings, lead author Dr. Arno Bourgonje said: "It is fascinating to see that complicated CD at diagnosis is associated with a distinct antibody profile years before the first clinical symptoms and is not simply the consequence of disease progression after diagnosis. Finding these patterns so early points to the potential of antibody profiling to support earlier risk detection, distinguish between disease subtypes and help identify patients who may benefit from more intensive therapy as early as possible."

Could a Blood Test Detect Gut Disease 10 Years Early?

Although the results offer compelling evidence that IBD has a detectable early immune signature, the researchers emphasize that the findings are not yet ready for use in routine medical screening.

The study establishes an important proof of principle, but additional research is necessary to determine whether these antibody patterns can reliably predict disease in broader populations.

Researchers must also establish whether antibody testing provides meaningful benefits beyond existing genetic information, clinical assessments, and other blood-based measurements. Any potential screening test would need to be accurate, affordable, reproducible, and ultimately shown to improve patient outcomes.

"The next priority is to validate these signatures in independent, more diverse and prospectively followed populations," concluded Dr. Bourgonje. "We also need to determine their added value alongside genetic, clinical and other blood-based markers, translate the findings into a reproducible and affordable targeted assay and, ultimately, demonstrate that using such a test actually leads to better clinical outcomes."

If future studies confirm these results, blood-based immune profiling could offer doctors a new way to recognize inflammatory bowel disease risk years before diagnosis, distinguish between disease subtypes, and identify patients who might benefit from earlier intervention.

#5708. Abdakibart Shows Strong Early Efficacy in Hidradenitis Suppurativa

— Phase II LOTUS data suggest IL-1 beta inhibition could become an important new approach

Phase II findings presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology meeting in Vienna showed promising early efficacy with abdakibart, an investigational interleukin (IL)-1 beta inhibitor, in patients with hidradenitis suppurativa (HS).

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Martina J. Porter, MD, of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, discusses the week-16 LOTUS trial results, including Hidradenitis Suppurativa Clinical Response 75 (HiSCR75) rates, early separation from placebo, the study's safety profile, and what the findings may mean as the drug moves into phase III.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

I was fortunate to present the phase II findings for the abdakibart study, which was by Avalo Therapeutics. Abdakibart is an IL-1 beta inhibitor. And what we showed was the week-16 or the primary endpoint results for the study. And this was one of the largest studies that we've seen for phase II to date. There were over 240 patients, about 80 in each arm, and there were two different abdakibart doses and then a placebo group.

The key point here was that HiSCR75, which is our higher depth of response, it was about 43% of patients in both of the dosing arms that achieved HiSCR75 compared to about 25% of placebo patients. And this is one of the highest, I would say, efficacy endpoints that we've seen to date for any HS phase II study. And I think it really validates that this is a novel mechanism that will probably be involved in treating HS going forward.

And I think some of the other important things, too, that we found were that there was actually quite an early split between the drug arms and the placebo group. So even as early as week 4, there was a difference in almost all the endpoints that we were talking about for the study.

Also for the 16 weeks, there were almost no safety findings at all for this IL-1 beta, which is actually very promising. A lot of times we get really concerned about HS patients, who have so many comorbidities, but there weren't any increased infection risks, for example. There were some injection site reactions, but they happened across all the groups, both the placebo and the abdakibart arms, to the same degree. And the most common side effects that we saw were things that are probably unlikely related to the drug, like headaches. So I think in terms of safety profiles, which are really important to dermatologists, this was quite clean for the 16 weeks.

So I think the important implications of this is that we'll see this molecule move into phase III and we'll also be able to see over a longer-term period -- so not just 16 weeks -- how it performs. And historically for all of our drugs in HS, we really like to see key differentiation and efficacy endpoints and clean safety profiles at week 16. But as we know for HS in general, it's also a lot about how these patients do long term at 6 months and 12 months and even longer because a lot of the times what we see is continued improvement in their disease severity over these periods, especially after we move out of the placebo response.

#5707. Nabrawind’s Crane-Free Wind Towers Face a Supplier Test

Spain’s Nabrawind has developed a way to install exceptionally tall wind turbine towers without bringing an enormous crawler crane to the site. Its Nabralift system uses a tubular upper tower supported by a three-legged steel structure. Hydraulic equipment raises the assembled turbine while modular sections are inserted below it near ground level. The lifting frame can then be removed and used on another installation. This addresses genuine logistical and construction problems, particularly at remote sites where specialist cranes are expensive to transport and where wind can interrupt conventional lifting operations.

The company has progressed beyond demonstration-scale hardware. In September 2026, UL Solutions issued type certification for Envision’s 7.8 MW turbine on Nabrawind’s 188-meter tower. Fortescue is using 17 of those tower configurations at the 133 MW Nullagine wind project in Western Australia’s Pilbara region, where construction is underway. Nabrawind previously erected a 160-meter prototype in Spain in under two weeks and has supplied smaller commercial towers in Morocco and France.

The engineering benefits are credible. Nabrawind reports using roughly 20% less tower steel than comparable conventional tubular designs and reducing foundation concrete by as much as 80%, depending on the design and site. Those are supplier claims rather than independently established savings across all wind farms. The potential to avoid large cranes, simplify transport and raise turbines in windier conditions could also matter substantially to total installed cost and construction schedules. High hub heights only earn their keep when those costs are justified by the electricity generated over the project’s life.

The current deployment has an unusual commercial structure. Fortescue acquired Nabrawind in September 2025 and is building Nullagine to serve its own mining operations. Fortescue has the capital, internal electricity demand and industrial incentive to support a technology it owns. Successful installation in that context would be important evidence of construction performance, but it would not establish that an unrelated wind developer can finance and maintain the same system under ordinary third-party commercial arrangements.

Nabralift’s proprietary construction approach creates a procurement issue. Conventional tubular towers can be sourced from several qualified manufacturers, and experienced contractors can compete for much of their construction work. A developer selecting Nabralift currently depends on one supplier for the core tower system, specialist lifting knowledge and associated support. Wind turbine original-equipment manufacturers also create supplier dependencies, but concentrating another critical part of the project in a proprietary installation system requires its own contract and risk assessment.

A type certificate provides valuable technical assurance about the certified turbine-and-tower configuration. A lender or insurer still needs enforceable delivery schedules, long-term warranties, repair and maintenance provisions, clarity on replacement parts, and a workable remedy if the supplier’s capacity or commercial priorities change. These questions become more important when a wind farm must operate for 25 years or longer and there is no qualified alternative provider of the same system.

Nabrawind’s next important proof point is an independently developed and financed large wind farm that accepts those risks on commercial terms. Qualified installation partners, credible long-term service arrangements and greater competitive capacity could make its engineering advantages easier for developers to buy. The 188-meter tower has earned technical attention; its broader market depends on financing and procurement confidence catching up with the machinery.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Nabrawind’s self-erecting design, Fortescue’s Nullagine deployment and the supplier concentration that independent wind developers would have to manage. It follows my earlier assessment of 300-meter wind towers, where construction economics were the central challenge.

#5706. BMW Just Went 186 MPH In The New Alpina 7 Series

Thanks to spy shots, we already knew BMW was hard at work cooking up the next Alpina B7 and that it'll have a V8 that sounds pretty great. The brand has now come out with official footage of the car doing high-speed testing at the Nardò test track, exceeding 186 mph. What, did you think the special label version of BMW's flagship sedan would be slow? For reference, the last-gen Alpina B7 already had a top speed of 205 mph, so 186 was frankly table stakes. That said, the speed itself arguably isn't what BMW is flexing her — it's the peace with which that speed is achieved.

"Speed has always been baked into the Alpina brand's DNA," said BMW Alpina vice president Oliver Viellechner. "However, we are not just interested in top speed alone. What matters is how natural, stable and confident it feels to drive at that speed." Internally, the brand apparently calls these cars "distance-shrinking" machines; autobahn weapons made to cover literal continents in great speed, style, and serenity.

You might recognize the name Nardò, by the way, from "Nardo Gray," that primer-like paint color popularized by Audi. The Nardò Ring, a 7.8-mile test track in southern Italy owned by Porsche and shaped like a perfect circle, is where that comes from.

Other confirmed details now include Alpina-signature 20-spoke lightweight wheels (peeping at the sidewall shows a diameter of 22 inches) wearing specially made tires that feature an extra layer of foam inside allowing for peak high-speed stability and comfort. Four oval exhaust tips emit a "rich, deep sound," and BMW says max torque out of that V8 is available "across virtually the entire rev range," while engine management software and throttle mapping is tweaked for smoothness over aggression. Gearbox tuning, too, has been revised to accommodate the bump in horsepower and engine speeds.

This new B7 (or whatever BMW will choose to call the next Alpina-ized 7 Series) will be the first production car made under the joint BMW Alpina brand. BMW announced that it had acquired Alpina back in 2022, but didn't take full control over the tuner until the beginning of this year. The new BMW Alpina 7 Series will be unveiled next year.

#5704. Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?

A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.

Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.

The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.

How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure

The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.

By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.

The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.

Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients

The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.

Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.

Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.

The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.

However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.

Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension

Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.

A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.

This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.

Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:

"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.

"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."

A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.

Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.

This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.

Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.

For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

#5703. Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn

Post-midterms, hospitals still face a long road to policy relief, advisers warn" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hospitals facing major policy headwinds won’t be able to sustain operations through cost cutting or revenue protections alone, and they shouldn’t bank on immediate political relief following this week’s midterm results, BRG policy and health system operations consultants warn.

Health systems across the country have been gearing up for the years-long rollout of Medicare and Medicaid policy changes from 2025’s H.R. 1, whose standout changes, such as Medicaid work requirements and state-directed payment restrictions, will begin in earnest on Jan. 1. The implementation is expected to reduce the number of patients with coverage and limit supplemental payments to providers, compounding challenges they’re already facing this year after expired Affordable Care Act subsidies pushed many patients off marketplace coverage.

“I’m generally an optimist as [my] personality, but the quote that comes to me is ‘It can never be so bad that it can’t get worse,” David Wildebrandt, a managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said during a Thursday media roundtable on federal policy takeaways for healthcare providers. “It’s really very troubling, the cumulative toll of everything that’s happening, because health systems have an incredibly difficult ecosystem in general in terms of capacity constraints, payer mix, softer volumes.”

Those headwinds will land amid a midterm election in which healthcare issues are top items for voters. Reversing or hobbling H.R. 1 has emerged as a priority for Democratic candidates and party leaders, promises that would have no small impact on hospitals hoping for a financial lifeline.

“I do think the biggest ticket item here for the next couple of years is how One Big Beautiful Bill Act implementation goes, how states respond and whether or not Congress tries to have a say by potentially trying to amend that bill in the first couple of years,” John Barkett, managing director in BRG’s Healthcare Transactions and Strategy practice, and formerly an advisor on the White House Domestic Policy Council, said. “It's not uncommon for big bills, including Obamacare or Medicare or any other big bill, to be amended within a couple of years of passage.”

In a scenario where Democrats take both the House (currently considered very likely by pollsters) and the Senate (more of a toss-up), BRG’s healthcare practice advisors said they anticipate a slew of new congressional oversight and investigations into health agencies and some of the organizations they’d cut deals with in recent years. And even if they can’t get a partisan health bill signed into law, there’s still room to write and pass bills that could become new policy in a future majority, as was the case with Medicaid work requirements pushed by Republicans during the end of the Biden administration but ultimately codified last year.

As for the OBBBA, the BRG consultants acknowledged that revisions to the sweeping Medicaid changes are possible, but pointed out the steep hill they’d need to climb.

“President Trump will still be president, and he will view a policy that amends the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in favor of hospitals as a concession to Democrats—and therefore, he’ll be looking for something in return,” Barkett said. “And so the question will be—how big is the ask for what the Trump administration would want in return for amending a signature law … and what he’s asking for would have to be palatable for Democrats. And that’s where I think there’s a lot of uncertainty right now.”

“Providers shouldn’t really plan on relief coming from Washington in that way,” Dave Brueggeman, another managing director in BRG’s healthcare practice, said of an OBBBA amendment and a potential swift return of marketplace subsidies.

Barkett noted that second-term, lame duck presidents tend to look at their legacy as lawmaking grinds to a halt. That could make Trump and his administration “even more emboldened to take action through [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid] rulemaking,” he said.

“The question I’m thinking about is—what signals is the president giving about what he wants his legacy to be on healthcare in the last couple of years,” he said. “I’m not sure that anyone who’s saying they know what that is necessarily has the mind of the president. I think it could go in several directions, and it’s particularly interesting given that the Supreme Court … has been constricting what an executive branch can do when they’re thinking creatively about how to interpret statutes.”

Should Republicans maintain control of The Hill, Barkett said the industry should expect a continuation of the policy agenda from the past two years—reduced coverage, lower spending and deference to regulatory agencies—with “maybe some bipartisan work going on,” such as pharmacy benefit manager reforms from earlier this year.

“The bottom line here is that revenue pressure from the OBBBA isn't a one-year problem,” said Brueggeman. “It builds over the next decade, and the systems that come out of it in best shape will be the ones that start adjusting the revenue and cost strategies now.”

The policy landscape is unprecedented ground for management teams that, likely for the first time in their careers, are facing a year in which overall health insurance coverage isn't increasing.

Wildebrandt's chief advice, based on best practices BRG is seeing among big names like HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare, is to cut through the unknowns and develop a financial exposure plan with “very sophisticated predictions of what's going to happen with charity care, uncompensated care, the amount of uninsured, EBITDA forecasts."

“The one thing I would certainly want to impress upon everyone is [that] it is different for every hospital. You cannot use a blanket statement,” he said of the policy impacts going into effect. Such predictions “really create a true north for everyone to look at. […] Some of the systems that are doing that, it’s been very much an awakening event.”

The immediate next priority, Wildebrandt said, is for systems to model and protect enrollment among patients who will still be eligible for coverage after January’s work requirements implementation deadline, for instance by “standing up outreach centers to help with the documentation and the education of the work requirements.” Brueggeman similarly raised red flags over yet-to-be-shared state guidance on how the changes could impact Medicaid presumptive eligibility, and noted that many BRG hospital clients are reviewing their collections and self-pay and charity care policies amid an expectation of increased payment difficulties.

From there, health systems will need to begin ramping up their cost optimization and strategic realignment, likely to a greater extent than what they’ve already pursued over the past year.

“What we share with our clients and folks that are really getting ahead of this is another 5% to 7% of cost reduction on top of what they're already doing,” he said. “And that really gets you into deeper areas beyond labor, beyond supply chain. What we're working on mostly is a transformational roadmap.”

The chief opportunities here, he said, involve integrated care models and leaning into many of the skills systems developed under risk-based arrangements to direct patients to community providers or other lower-cost settings when possible.

“We’ll likely see an explosion of growth in partnerships with FQHCs and other community organizations to get folks into the right care setting and reduce unnecessary utilization,” he said. “And another important area, one we’ve honestly given some lip service to over time, is partnering to expand ambulatory access and, again, reduce preventable hospital use.”

Wildebrandt described these efforts as requiring “structural changes” addressing “fixed costs, and not just working into variable costs.” That means taking a hard look at what’s currently on offer.

“We see many organizations assessing their portfolio, looking at service rationalization—especially big systems that have integrated and have redundant OB units within the same perimeter,” he said. “You'll see more Centers of Excellence coming out of this, which will decrease access, but consolidating services, OB, pediatric intensive care units, and other non-core programs like post-acute rehab. … You’re seeing folks also spinning things off, spinning hospitals off, spinning service lines off. So definitely a lot of activity in this space.”

Leaders from major nonprofit health systems who were on the panel agreed. Matt Brown, president of CommonSpirit Health’s South Region, said it’s become more routine to hear of cost-conscious systems targeting stiffer benchmarks for their labor spending—salary, wages and benefits expenses below 45% of patient service revenue, “when 15 years ago under 60% was appropriate."

He and Gail Kosyla, chief financial officer at AtlantiCare, also acknowledged that nonprofits are already weighing options on service lines that are losing money for the system, noting that providers could mitigate the impact on patient access by partnering with another community provider already offering the same services.

“Those are difficult decisions, and they really go to patient need, community need, as well as that financial component,” Kosyla said during the roundtable.

With the scope of headwinds to come, panelists agreed that cost management alone won't close the gap without corresponding efforts to protect revenue.

Brueggeman said his team has been working “every day” on an “explosive growth” in termination planning, as providers negotiating new network agreements with payers are increasingly willing to play chicken in order to maximize revenue. Should those disputes come to a head, a hospital’s network exit could mean reduced access to care for local patients.

Brueggeman noted that the contentious negotiations have recently lost a natural common ground. Risk-based arrangements with shared upsides and downsides have become less appealing to providers due to a “lack of ability to specifically predict what those outcomes would look like,” with the policy changes, he said. “That creates a significant tension against what was, at one time, considered an outlet in these negotiations of creating a shared responsibility around risk. It's creating a little bit of a dam in that process.”

CommonSpirit’s Brown was up front about the need to go toe-to-toe, and the benefits for doing so.

“We’re doing everything we can with payers to understand how we maximize our reimbursement,” he said. “That means draconian things at times. We’ve had markets go out of network with Medicare Advantage providers. And we’ve gotten back in recently—specifically a community in Texas. We went out for a while and then came back in as a national player.”

“We have to do everything we can to leverage our scale in negotiations with payers—and with states to ensure that we don't get hit with provider fee problems in places like Kentucky, Colorado and California to the level that H.R. 1 projects,” he added.

#5702. GM Recalls Over 67,000 Chevy Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, And Even Celestiqs For Temporary Loss Of Braking

General Motors is recalling 67,380 Chevrolet Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, and even Celestiqs because under specific circumstances, a software defect can cause a temporary loss of braking ability. According to the NHTSA recall report, GM is aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries. Fortunately, the condition only arises at low speeds, but any loss of braking is a deeply concerning and dangerous occurrence. Two-wheel-drive Cadillac Lyriqs are not included in the recall, and the only Blazer EV trims involved are SS and Police Pursuit Vehicles.

Cadillac Lyriqs are hit hardest by the recall, which includes 474 2023 Lyriqs, 22,819 2024 Lyriqs, 11,926 2025 Lyriqs, 9,322 2026 Lyriqs, and 44 2027 Lyriqs. The recall also includes 13,627 2026 Vistiqs and 5,175 2027 Vistiqs, as well as 51 2025 Celestiqs, and 31 2026 Celestiqs. (This is one of our best glimpses yet into how many Celestiqs have been sold.) The only Chevrolets included in the recall are 562 2024 Blazer EVs, 2012 2025 Blazer EVs, 1,314 2026 Blazer EVs, and 23 2027 Blazer EVs. VINs are already searchable on NHTSA's website, and the remedy comes in the form of an over-the-air update for owners who have opted in to those, otherwise owners will have to take their vehicles to dealerships to have the software update downloaded.

The conditions that lead to the temporary loss of brake function are very specific. According to the recall report and GM's testing, "when the brakes are lightly applied at low speeds during a sharp turn and the vehicle encounters a bump or depression – such as at the end of a driveway – a momentary release and reapplication of the brakes may cause the software's slip calculation to misinterpret wheel movement. In some instances, this may result in a temporary loss of braking. The phenomenon is unique to certain vehicles equipped with performance all-wheel drive (pAWD, RPO X0E) and is resolved when the brakes are applied again."

GM already recalled 21,469 all-wheel-drive Lyriqs for a similar issue in 2024, but it found that vehicles built with the software changes following that recall and vehicles that already received the software update from that recall are still susceptible to the conditions described in the new recall, and they need the latest update. The latest software update corrects the slip calculation in the vehicle's brake system control module that causes the temporary loss of braking, which coincidentally is the same claim made on the 2024 recall. Hopefully this time it actually fixes the problem.

If you drive one of the cars included in the recall, be aware of the possibility of braking loss, and remember that if you experience braking loss, normal brake function should return on the next brake press. Dealers should already be notified of the recall, but owner notification is estimated to begin on December 14.

Cancer care is shifting beyond the detection of visible disease. #5700. Cancer Vaccines Show Promise. But We Have More Work to Do.

— A look at how individualized cancer vaccines may fit into a complex treatment landscape

The controversy surrounding the premature disclosure of Moderna and Merck's mRNA melanoma vaccine results risks overshadowing a more consequential clinical discussion: how individualized cancer vaccines might fit into an increasingly effective and increasingly complex treatment landscape.

The results are very encouraging. Reducing recurrence and distant metastases by adding a treatment with a new mechanism to an effective checkpoint inhibitor represent meaningful progress. Our work now is to determine which patients benefit, how vaccination should be sequenced with other treatments, and whether its promise extends beyond melanoma.

In INTerpath-001, which randomized 1,137 patients with completely resected stage IIB–IV melanoma, results presented at ESMO showed 2-year recurrence-free survival of 82.2% with the mRNA-based cancer vaccine intismeran autogene plus pembrolizumab (Keytruda) versus 70% with placebo plus pembrolizumab. The absolute difference was 12.2 percentage points; the hazard ratio was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.45-0.75). At a median follow-up of 24.6 months, an overall survival benefit had not been demonstrated.

Preventing recurrence has clinical value. It can spare patients further treatment and morbidity. But not all patients benefited from the intervention, and these findings do not establish efficacy across other cancers.

The biological rationale behind intismeran autogene is compelling. Personalized mRNA vaccines encode tumor-specific neoantigens that antigen-presenting cells process and present to prime and expand tumor-reactive T cells. PD-1 blockade complements this response by reducing inhibitory signaling that limits T-cell activity. Vaccination may therefore broaden tumor-directed immunity while checkpoint inhibition supports its function. INTerpath-001 demonstrates the benefit of adding vaccination to pembrolizumab; without a vaccine-only arm, it cannot formally establish synergy.

This approach brings together tumor sequencing, computational antigen selection, mRNA delivery, and immunotherapy. Yet a predicted neoantigen is not necessarily an effective immune target. Translational studies must clarify which responses control the cancer clones responsible for recurrence.

The vaccine discussion also needs to account for progress in neoadjuvant immunotherapy. In SWOG S1801, beginning pembrolizumab before surgery improved event-free survival compared with administering it entirely afterward. In NADINA, neoadjuvant nivolumab-ipilimumab followed by surgery and response-directed postoperative therapy improved event-free survival compared with surgery followed by nivolumab (Opdivo).

These advances make sequencing a central research question. Could vaccination improve outcomes after neoadjuvant immunotherapy? Might patients without a major pathological response have the greatest need? Conversely, could patients with a major response avoid additional treatment?

INTerpath-001 does not answer these questions. Nor can cross-trial comparisons, as populations, endpoints, and treatment strategies differ. The neoadjuvant question is particularly relevant to patients with clinically apparent, resectable stage III disease; it should not obscure the vaccine findings in other patients represented in the trial.

We need studies that integrate advances in treatment rather than simply accumulate postoperative therapies. Residual disease after checkpoint inhibition also does not necessarily imply vaccine sensitivity. That hypothesis requires testing.

Beyond melanoma, our optimism must remain tempered by the evidence. Tumors differ in antigen availability, antigen presentation, immune infiltration, and mechanisms of immune suppression. Still, early findings justify investigation and enthusiasm. A phase I pancreatic cancer study demonstrated persistent vaccine-induced T-cell responses in some patients receiving an individualized mRNA vaccine alongside atezolizumab and chemotherapy. Immune responders had longer recurrence-free survival than nonresponders.

This establishes biological activity, not that vaccination improves outcomes in pancreatic cancer. The study was small, lacked a randomized control group, and compared patients according to their immune response. A randomized trial is evaluating the combination more rigorously.

Patient selection deserves similar discipline. Pathological response and circulating tumor DNA are attractive candidates for refining postoperative decisions. But identifying patients at higher risk of recurrence is different from identifying those more likely to benefit from vaccination. Biomarker-guided treatment strategies require prospective evaluation.

Delivery is another clinical endpoint in practice. In INTerpath-001, vaccine production was successful for more than 99% of patients assigned to intismeran, an encouraging feasibility result. Median time to the first vaccine dose was 64 days. That interval is not simply a manufacturing-time estimate, but it makes treatment coordination -- and the feasibility of preoperative vaccination -- important research questions.

Safety also requires attention. Grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 14.2% of patients receiving intismeran plus pembrolizumab versus 13.4% of those receiving pembrolizumab alone. However, all-cause adverse events led to discontinuation of any study drug in 16.6% versus 9.5%, respectively. Similar rates of severe treatment-related toxicity do not establish an identical treatment burden.

Regulators must evaluate manufacturing consistency alongside efficacy and safety. Clinicians need durable outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and practical delivery data. Health systems must determine whether treatment is feasible and affordable beyond specialized centers.

As an oncologist working in clinical development and global cancer care, I would place access within the development agenda from the beginning. Adequate tissue, sequencing capacity, production infrastructure, and coverage and reimbursement will determine who benefits.

Personalized cancer vaccines could become an important component of perioperative treatment. Their greatest contribution may come through careful integration with checkpoint inhibition, response assessment, and better patient selection. Our responsibility is to translate an encouraging result into longer and better lives, while avoiding unnecessary treatment, toxicity, and financial burden.

#5699. Bay Area Air District Moves Forward with Nation’s Strongest Water Heater Standards

Health advocates, environmental groups, heat pump installers, local electeds celebrate decision as.

SAN FRANCISCO — The Bay Area Air District voted today to move forward with the strongest clean appliance standards in the nation, putting millions of Bay Area homes on a path to switch from gas water heaters to zero-emission alternatives. Beginning in 2028, households will be required to install water heater appliances that meet clean air standards as old gas units burn out, with exemptions approved today for low-income households and complicated installations.

Gas appliances in Bay Area homes and buildings generate more smog-forming nitrogen oxide pollution than all of the region’s passenger cars combined. The Air District estimates its clean appliance standards for water heaters and furnaces could prevent up to 85 premature deaths and 15,000 asthma attacks each year.

The switch also saves families money. New research from RMI finds $360 in annual savings for Bay Area residents from switching from gas water heater to a heat pump. Analysis from SPUR projects $315 million in rebates for home energy efficiency will be available in the next three years to support the transition.

The vote follows thousands of public comments in support of the standards, despite an industry-backed opposition campaign linked to oil interests.

Supporters of the standards released the following statements:

“The research makes it clear that climate policies and affordability go hand-in-hand and today the Bay Area is taking the historic step of making clean home appliances the standard for a better future,” said Melissa Yu, Campaign Strategist for Clean Heat, Sierra Club. “A transition toward zero-emission gas heaters will reduce a key source of smog pollution, launch programs to help get more people access better technological solutions and lower energy costs. Today’s vote is a victory for cleaner air and for energy affordability.”

“Today’s vote will supercharge the job growth we’re already seeing at heat pump businesses like mine, opening new pathways for early-career Bay Area workers looking for family-sustaining wages and meaningful work. The Bay Area Air District showed real leadership in approving these standards. We’re proud to be on the front lines of equipping homes with energy-efficient technologies that cut energy bills, clean the air, and make homes more comfortable,” said Owen Krebs Grimsich, CEO and owner of 1-888 Heat Pumps.

“Today, the Bay Area chose clean air over fossil fuel pollution. Under these standards, when a household’s gas water heater wears out, it will be replaced with cleaner, more efficient technology like a heat pump, so millions of residents will breathe easier and save money on their energy bills. The Bay Area Air District showed real leadership, and the rest of the country should follow its lead,” said Tony Sirna, Deputy Policy Director for Buildings at Evergreen Action.

“Today’s vote is a big win for clean air, lower utility bills, and climate leadership,” said Berkeley City Council member Igor Tregub. “The Bay Area is moving forward with the nation’s strongest water heater standards, and millions of families here will breathe cleaner air as a result. These standards build in the flexibility we need to make the transition workable, while growing the market for clean technologies that lower bills and create good jobs.”

“Today, the Bay Area Air District said yes to saving lives and no to gas industry attempts to slow progress to clean our air,” said Fernando Gaytan, senior attorney on Earthjustice’s Right To Zero campaign. “The Bay Area is now one step closer to making non-polluting appliances the  norm thanks to the leadership of board members and staff. This policy will show the rest of the country what’s possible.”

“Today’s vote is a step forward for cleaner air, healthier homes, and a more affordable energy future. By advancing these standards, the Air District shows we can move away from polluting gas appliances without leaving families behind,” said Sam Fishman, sustainability and resilience policy manager, SPUR. “Bay Area cities, utilities, and regional programs are taking the important steps to invest more than $120 million annually in home electrification and energy-efficiency incentives. With these tools, we can make our homes safer for our planet and our health, too.”

“As regional leaders in building electrification, Acterra sees this vote as a vital win for local communities and public health,” said Lauren Weston, Executive Director at Acterra: Action for a Healthy Planet. “Transitioning to zero-emission heat pump water heaters clears toxic nitrogen oxide pollution from our neighborhoods while lowering utility bills and accelerating equitable access to clean, energy-efficient technology for all Bay Area households.”

“The Air District Board’s vote today to support the implementation of Rule 9-6 is a watershed victory for healthy and safe communities, moving from our dependence on fossil fuels to a cleaner, greener source of energy,” said Leslie Alden, Executive Director of Act Now Bay Area. “The Air District staff, the experts, the working groups, and so many dedicated members representing the Bay Area worked tirelessly from 2023 show once again that the Bay Area leads the way.”
