#5686. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."

#5685. Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication

Missing doses of blood pressure medication could significantly reduce its ability to protect against heart attacks, strokes, and other serious cardiovascular problems, according to findings presented at ESC Congress 2026.

An estimated 1.4 billion adults worldwide between the ages of 30 and 79 have high blood pressure (hypertension), a major contributor to illness and death. Although medications that lower blood pressure are proven to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications, approximately half of patients do not take their prescriptions as directed.

"We have evidence that poor adherence to antihypertensive medication is associated with worse outcomes," explained presenter, Miss Qianqian Yang from the University of Oxford, UK. "However, previous data has come from observational studies and could be confounded by other factors. We undertook an analysis of randomized trial data to assess the true impact of adherence on the benefits of antihypertensive treatment."

Major Study Examines the Impact of Missed Blood Pressure Medication

To better understand how consistently taking medication affects its benefits, researchers analyzed individual patient data from 91,339 participants across nine clinical trials. Each trial compared a blood pressure treatment (intervention group) with an alternative approach (comparator group: either placebo or a less-intensive regimen).

The researchers divided participants into two categories based on how closely they followed their prescribed treatment. Those who took at least 80% of their assigned medication were considered to have higher adherence, while those who took less than 80% were placed in the lower adherence group.

Even with the regular monitoring and structured conditions of clinical trials, patients became less consistent about taking their medication as time passed.

"A decline in adherence over time was apparent, even in the structured setting of trials," noted Miss Yang. Overall, 88% of participants met the higher adherence threshold during the first year, but that figure had dropped to just 79% by the fifth year.

Skipping Blood Pressure Pills Reduces Treatment Benefits

The difference in medication adherence was reflected in how much patients' blood pressure improved.

Among participants with higher adherence, systolic blood pressure, the top number in a blood pressure reading, was 5.2 mmHg lower in the intervention group than in the comparator group. For those with lower adherence, the difference was considerably smaller at just 3.0 mmHg.

Researchers then examined whether these differences translated into protection against major cardiovascular problems. The outcomes included strokes, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), ischemic heart disease, and heart failure that resulted in hospitalization or death.

The findings revealed a striking contrast. Among patients who consistently followed their treatment plans, the intervention group experienced an 11% lower incidence of major cardiovascular events compared with the comparator group. However, among patients with lower adherence, there was no statistically significant reduction in these events.

"Notably, our results reinforce the saying that 'drugs don't work in patients who don't take them.' Patients with lower adherence derived little or no cardiovascular benefit, whereas those with higher adherence had greater reductions in blood pressure and prevention of cardiovascular events," said Miss Yang.

Helping Patients Get Lifesaving Heart Protection

The researchers believe that helping people take their medication consistently should become a greater priority in the treatment of high blood pressure. They recommend more routine assessments of medication adherence, along with better patient education and practical strategies to make treatment easier to follow.

Possible approaches include simplifying medication schedules, combining multiple treatments into a single pill, and prescribing longer-acting drugs that can help limit the consequences of an occasional missed dose.

Professor Felix Mahfoud, Chair of the ESC Communication Committee, emphasized that missed medication has received too little attention as a contributor to poorly controlled blood pressure.

"For years, we have neglected non-adherence to medication as a cause for uncontrolled hypertension. Assessment of adherence should become a routine part of hypertension care so patients do not miss out on life-saving benefits. As healthcare providers, we are here to have open, non-judgmental conversations with our patients about any barriers they may have to taking medication, to help improve adherence."

Materials provided by European Society of Cardiology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5684. Brain Health Linked With Longer Lifetime Estrogen Exposure

— Menopausal hormone therapy tied to lower cerebral small vessel disease burden, study shows

Women with higher lifetime estrogen exposure had less cerebrovascular pathology, a cohort study in Sweden showed.

A longer reproductive span was associated with 8% lower odds of having two or more signs of cerebral small vessel disease (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.99), reported Anna Marseglia, PhD, of the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and co-authors.

Menopausal hormone therapy was also linked with lower cerebral small vessel disease burden (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20-0.81) and with increasing white matter integrity (ß=0.28, 95% CI 0.06-0.50), Marseglia and colleagues wrote in Neurology.

Among APOE4 carriers only, menopausal hormone therapy was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions typically affected by Alzheimer's disease (β=0.38, 95% CI 0.01-0.76).

Women who used oral contraceptives earlier in life and menopausal hormone therapy later had the lowest small vessel disease burden (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.83) and the greatest white matter integrity (β=0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.78), the researchers said.

"What was particularly striking was that the most favorable vascular brain health was observed among women who had used oral contraceptives during their reproductive years and later received menopausal hormone therapy. This suggests that hormonal factors acting across different stages of a woman's life may have cumulative associations with cerebrovascular health in older age," Marseglia said in a statement.

"While these findings do not establish cause and effect, they underscore the importance of considering women's reproductive and hormonal history when studying brain aging and dementia risk, not only in relation to Alzheimer's disease but also to vascular disease," she added.

The role of endogenous and exogenous estrogen exposure in brain health may be an opportunity to identify dementia mechanisms, observed Tracy Madsen, MD, PhD, of the University of Vermont in Burlington.

"The lifetime risk of dementia in U.S. women exceeds that of men, and recent projections suggest that by 2060, the number of incident dementia cases in women will surpass that of men by 233,000," Madsen wrote in an accompanying editorial.

The link between estrogen exposure and brain health has become more important with the FDA's recent removal of its black box warning from menopausal hormone therapy, Madsen pointed out. "Furthermore, the idea of reproductive lifespan and ovarian longevity as a potential modifiable target is a critical concept for women's health," she wrote.

Early research suggested that menopausal hormone therapy might protect against Alzheimer's and cardiovascular disease, but in 2003, the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS) reported that estrogen-plus-progestin formulations increased probable dementia risk in women ages 65 or older. The Women's Health Initiative trial also linked combined estrogen and progestin to higher breast cancer and heart disease risks, leading to black box warnings which the FDA removed in 2026.

Over time, the use of hormone replacement therapy in the U.S. declined among postmenopausal women from 26.9% in 1999 to 4.7% in 2020. The treatment is still considered controversial.

More recently, autopsy data and other research have linked estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy with reduced Alzheimer's neuropathology and lower odds of a dementia diagnosis. A large U.K. Biobank study also suggested that starting hormone replacement therapy early was associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's and dementia.

In their study, Marseglia and colleagues assessed 352 cognitively unimpaired women from the 1944 Gothenburg H70 birth cohort study who had brain MRI at age 70. Of these, 286 participated in a follow-up exam 5 years later.

The mean Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 29.2 at baseline, indicating normal cognitive function. About one-third (31%) of the cohort were APOE4 carriers.

Reproductive lifespan was calculated by subtracting the age at menarche from the age at menopause or oophorectomy. Study outcomes included cerebral small vessel disease, Alzheimer's-related cortical thickness, and white matter integrity. Small vessel disease burden was a composite score derived from white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, cerebral microbleeds, and perivascular spaces.

On average, women had a reproductive lifespan of 37.1 years. Most women (72.7%) reported using oral contraceptives; 60.8% reported using menopausal hormone therapy.

Longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time, the researchers said. Use of menopausal hormone therapy was linked with fewer perivascular spaces and cerebral microbleeds, they added.

Hormone exposure was reported by participants and may be subject to recall bias and misclassification, Marseglia and co-authors acknowledged. The study lacked detailed information about oral contraceptive and hormone therapy use.

#5682. Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think

Even alcohol consumption that many Americans would describe as moderate may carry significant health risks, including a greater likelihood of premature death, disability, cancer, and heart disease. That is the conclusion of a new study published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, a journal published at Rutgers University.

The research, known as the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, was originally commissioned by the U.S. federal government to help shape updated national dietary recommendations. Researchers estimated that people who consume an average of 14 alcoholic drinks per week face a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes. By comparison, consuming up to seven drinks weekly was linked to only small increases in risk for most health conditions.

"Even low levels of alcohol use come with health risks," says lead study author Kevin Shield, Ph.D., an associate professor at the University of Toronto and a senior scientist who leads the World Health Organization (WHO)/Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Collaborating Centre in Addiction and Mental Health. "And that risk continues to increase the more someone drinks."

How Scientists Measured the Health Risks of Alcohol

To better understand the long-term consequences of drinking, Shield and his colleagues in the United States and Canada investigated how alcohol consumption over a lifetime contributes to disease and premature death among Americans.

Medical experts first examined more than 7,200 scientific publications covering illnesses and injuries associated with alcohol. Using this evidence, they estimated the risks for individual health conditions and combined those findings with large national health data sets. Statistical models then allowed the team to calculate how different levels of alcohol consumption affect the likelihood of developing serious health problems or dying prematurely.

The findings provide specific estimates that are missing from the latest U.S. Dietary Guidelines. The updated recommendations simply encourage Americans to "limit alcoholic beverages" without identifying a particular consumption threshold. Earlier versions advised men to drink no more than two alcoholic beverages per day and women no more than one.

"While the new U.S. Dietary Guidelines contain a useful 'less-is-best' message, they provide no quantitative framework. Our study was designed to do just that across the drinking spectrum," says study co-author Timothy Naimi, M.D., M.P.H., director of the University of Victoria's Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research and an adjunct professor at Boston University.

"It turns out that two drinks per day, which might be considered 'moderate' from a social standpoint, is associated with a substantially elevated risk of a premature death caused by alcohol," explains Naimi.

Moderate Drinking Offers No Significant Overall Health Benefits

The researchers looked beyond the risk of premature death to examine alcohol's connection to a wide range of immediate and long-term health problems. These included cancers (e.g., esophageal, oral, and breast), cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and injuries.

One of the study's most important findings challenges the longstanding belief that consuming small amounts of alcohol can improve health, particularly heart health.

"We did not observe a significant protective effect of alcohol on health at any level of consumption," says Shield. "At low levels, alcohol may be associated with a reduced risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke. But when you look across the full range of health outcomes, including cancer and other chronic diseases, those potential benefits are outweighed by the risks even at 7 drinks per week."

In other words, while some studies have suggested that light drinking may benefit certain aspects of cardiovascular health, those possible advantages do not translate into an overall health benefit once alcohol's links to cancer and other diseases are taken into account.

Although the analysis drew on extensive scientific evidence, the researchers emphasize that its estimates describe risks across populations rather than predicting precisely what will happen to any particular person.

Shield says the statistical calculations relied on "the best possible data." However, he cautions that individual circumstances can substantially influence the results.

"However, we can't assume that means one person's individual health risk is the same as what is reported here -- that depends on other factors like lifestyle, genetics, drinking patterns, and other choices that differ person to person."

To estimate alcohol's overall impact, the researchers calculated risks for health conditions already known to be caused by alcohol and combined them into a broader assessment. However, scientists are continuing to investigate additional possible consequences of drinking, including emerging evidence connecting alcohol consumption to pancreatic cancer.

"Understanding those relationships, and how much alcohol contributes to those risks, is an area that still needs further work," says Shield.

What the Findings Mean for U.S. Drinking Guidelines

The results suggest that alcohol-related health risks become more pronounced when consumption exceeds one drink per day, regardless of whether the person is male or female. This provides a more specific reference point for people trying to understand how their drinking habits might affect their long-term health.

Rather than suggesting that any particular amount is completely safe, the findings show how risks increase with greater consumption and why drinking less generally reduces exposure to alcohol-related harm.

"Having a clearer threshold helps people better understand what level of drinking is associated with increased risk and make more informed decisions when drinking," says Shield.

The study has also raised questions about how scientific evidence was incorporated into federal dietary recommendations.

In an accompanying editorial, Robert M. Vincent, a former Associate Administrator for the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, offers his perspective on the circumstances surrounding the research and its role in the development of national guidance.

"The Alcohol Intake and Health report was explicitly invited to inform alcohol guidance during development of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030," he writes. "Despite the study's adherence to its mandate, its findings were sidelined."

Materials provided by Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The company said that it "chose to fast-track services that are widely considered in the medical community to be safe and effective," per the release. The changes will reduce prior authorization volume in pediatrics by nearly two-thirds, and apply across commercial, individual market and community plans where eligible under state law.

The changes aren't limited to services provided at pediatric facilities, UnitedHealthcare said.

Since then, the insurer has taken multiple steps to reduce the requirements on prior auth.

On Oct. 1, the company eliminated prior authorization on 1,700 services across its insurance lines. In May, UHC said it was aiming to eliminate 30% of prior auth requirements by the end of the year.

UnitedHealthcare is set to eliminate close to two-thirds of pediatric prior authorization requirements by the end of the year.

The insurance giant announced Friday morning that it will nix prior auth on an array of diagnostic tests, routine surgeries and specialty services, including cardiology, neurology, pulmonology and orthopedics.

UnitedHealth also said it will offer authorization waivers for certain procedures when they're performed at leading pediatric hospitals as a reflection of their "consistent use of well-established care practices." The insurer said that the facilities in this program represent a broad national network across medical and surgical specialties.

“Parents should be able to spend less time having to navigate the health system and more time focusing on their children as they get the care they need,” said Tim Noel, CEO of UnitedHealthcare, in the announcement.

“These changes are part of our broader efforts to simplify healthcare and allow families—and their doctors and nurses—to pursue routine care with far fewer administrative steps, while higher-risk procedures continue to undergo reviews," Noel added.

The company is undertaking a broad review of all pediatric prior authorizations to determine which can be rolled back while maintaining safety and quality. It said it plans to eliminate pre-approvals for some diagnostic imaging, sleep studies, routine outpatient tests and some surgical services and therapies that are approved consistently.

UnitedHealthcare said prior authorization will remain in place for services with high clinical complexity or variability, such as experimental treatments, or where it is required by regulations.

The company said the changes will take effect across its commercial and Medicaid plans.

The move is the latest from the company as it aims to reduce prior authorization requirements. For example, last month, UnitedHealth said it would exempt rural providers from most prior auth requirements.

The company has also made a push to reduce a wide swath of reauthorizations at its pharmacy benefit manager, Optum Rx.

#5680. AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis

An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."

Zocdoc opens infrastructure to AI agents, launches partnership with Instinct" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As more patients turn to artificial intelligence agents to manage their healthcare, Zocdoc is opening its healthcare access infrastructure to streamline the process.

Beginning Oct. 28, agents can connect patients to care through a variety of channels—including MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, deep links and more.

Zocdoc Chief Strategy Officer Alex Doyne told Fierce Healthcare that AI agents are “becoming a new starting point for patients seeking healthcare.”

Doyne said traffic from AI agents on the platform has “at least doubled roughly every three weeks since July.”

“AI agents can help patients navigate their healthcare options and take action on their behalf, but they're only as reliable as the information and systems they can access,” Doyne said. “By connecting agents to Zocdoc's infrastructure, we can ensure they are booking the right appointments for patients.”

Zocdoc has over 175 scheduling integrations, with more than 10,000 insurance plans and 200,000 verified providers in its network, according to Doyne.

“Opening that infrastructure to agents means they now have access to a reliable booking experience,” Doyne said.

Doyne added that healthcare is “particularly challenging,” for AI agents since “so much of the information available online is fragmented, outdated, or inaccurate,” which can have “real consequences for patients who may already be struggling to access care.”

“That's why it's critical that agents have access to reliable provider and insurance information, accurate availability and infrastructure that ensures the booking is integrated with a provider’s calendar and will hold on the day,” Doyne said.

“We've established a two-way promise that sets clear expectations for Zocdoc and the agents connecting to our infrastructure,” Doyne said. “Zocdoc commits to welcoming agents that register and identify themselves, while agents are expected to obtain explicit patient consent before booking appointments and protect patient and provider data.”

The company also announced a partnership with AI personal assistant Instinct to let agents use Zocdoc’s healthcare access infrastructure to find vetted providers, verify insurance benefits and book appointments.

“Instinct is built to genuinely improve your life and handle important everyday tasks,” said Ben Schwerin, Instinct chief business officer, in a statement. “Since healthcare is more complicated than ordering groceries or booking travel, the stakes are higher. By partnering with Zocdoc, Instinct can navigate that complexity—so getting an appointment can be as simple as sending a text.”

Instinct will join Zocdoc’s growing Care Access Network, which also includes Google Gemini, Amazon Health AI, Yelp, Healthgrades and more.

Last month, Zocdoc acquired Sohar Health in its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure.

Sohar Health helps healthcare organizations simplify insurance workflows, and its APIs automate insurance discovery, eligibility and benefits verification, network status checks and cost estimates.

It marked the company's first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history, executives said.

#5677. A Pediatrician, a Pastor, and a Paralympian Just Did Wonders for Kids’ Mental Health

— The midterm elections offer lessons in decency and difference

My son is 32. Early Wednesday morning he forwarded me a New York Times story about the new faces Tuesday's midterm elections sent to Washington and to statehouses.

He added a note: "Some themes for your next article, like the Knicks one. A message about being decent human beings. A message about how what makes us different brings us together." Then he quoted one line from the Times article: "There's a pediatrician, a pastor, a Paralympian and a former Navy helicopter pilot."

In June, I wrote that the Knicks' championship handed parents a teaching moment. My son was right: Tuesday handed us another.

Our kids and pediatric patients need the lesson. They have lived through a full campaign season. Attack ads. Comment sections. Adults yelling at screens. Before the last presidential election, 77% of American adults named the future of the nation a significant source of stress. Children absorb what we carry home. In the Trevor Project's 2024 national survey, 90% of LGBTQ+ young people said politics had hurt their well-being in the last year. Let's call that the un-teaching.

First, start with the line my son quoted. The pediatrician is Annie Andrews, MD, of South Carolina. She ran for the Senate on a platform focused on children's health after a 2025 measles outbreak sickened some 1,000 children in her state. Andrews, a pediatric hospitalist, saw harm to kids and asked for the job of stopping it.

The pastor is Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist congregation in the country. In January he was a registered Republican. Now he is the first Democrat to win a New Hampshire Senate seat in Kansas since 1932. He campaigned on his faith and promised to work across the aisle.

The Paralympian is Josh Turek of Iowa. Two gold medals in wheelchair basketball. A working-class kid. A man who once voted for George W. Bush. He is headed to the Senate.

The helicopter pilot is Rebecca Bennett. She flew for the Navy, ran a healthcare business, and now heads to the House from New Jersey.

Then come the firsts. Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black woman ever elected governor in this country. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will be the first openly gay man in the Senate; he told the Times he is living a life he could not have pictured as a boy. Abdul El-Sayed, MD, DPhil, of Michigan, a physician who ran Detroit's health department, will be the first Muslim senator. Melat Kiros, 29, becomes the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. James Talarico, a former middle-school teacher who quotes Scripture in his stump speech, will be the youngest member of the Senate at 37.

Ask a child what these people share. Different faiths. Different bodies. Different races, ages, loves, hometowns. Each one walked into rooms full of strangers and asked for their trust. The strangers said yes. What makes each of us different brought them together.

Talk about Amy Acton, MD, MPH. A physician, Ohio's former health director, now its governor-elect. She has spoken openly about a traumatic childhood and sexual abuse at the hand of her stepfather. Late in the race, an ad from her opponent put Acton's estranged mother on camera to call her a liar. Acton held her ground. She said she told her story so other people might see a way out.

As a child psychiatrist, I treat children with histories like hers. Most of them believe the worst thing that happened to them is the truest thing about them. Let's tell these patients Acton's story.

Adolescents build an identity partly by borrowing one. They pick role models whose life stories connect to their own, and they gravitate toward role models who resemble them. For some kids that is a matter of life and death. LGBTQ+ youth who have an older LGBTQ+ role model report lower rates of considering and attempting suicide. In an earlier Trevor survey, more than 80% said positive public role models made them feel better about who they are. A gay teenager in Manchester watched a gay man win a New Hampshire Senate seat Tuesday night. A kid in a wheelchair in Des Moines watched a Paralympian win one in Iowa. That registers.

Difference, met up close, heals. Cross-group friendships rank among the strongest known antidotes to prejudice in childhood, and they support children's well-being. Civic life protects too. In a national study that followed more than 9,000 adolescents into adulthood, those who volunteered and voted went on to have better mental health and engage in fewer risky behaviors. Community engagement in adolescence predicted fewer depressive symptoms years later.

My son also pointed out another crucial point: Kids across the country just witnessed an incredible underdog story. Talarico and El-Sayed were up against hundreds of millions of dollars in opposition spending. Several of the winning candidates represent groups historically left out from Congress, including gays, Blacks, Hispanics, and women. There is something immensely powerful about marginalized candidates running campaigns built around taking care of their communities and defeating the wealthiest individuals in the country. It doesn't matter how powerful you are, compassion for others and belief in self is what can change the world. That's a story our young patients need to witness.

Of course, half of the country may have woken up disappointed Wednesday. But even for that half, the lesson holds. Hamilton was a Republican 10 months ago. Turek voted for Bush. A child can admire a person and still argue with the platform. Disagreement is healthy. Contempt is the toxin. After the last election, the head of the American Psychological Association warned that pulling away from people over politics can cost us the relationships we need most.

Decency. Service. Faith worn in the open. Grit in a wheelchair. Honesty about one's own pain. A hand across the aisle. Strangers saying yes to someone unlike themselves.

There's the message. Everyone in this country has a reason to bring it up this week, and a son or daughter or patient will be ready to hear it.

My son is 32. He still sends me lessons. That's how it's supposed to work. Don't let the moment pass.

#5676. FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens

FTC issues warning letters over deceptive marketing as ACA enrollment opens" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Open enrollment season is getting underway, and the Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 25 companies that conduct marketing or generate sales leads for insurers.

The commission said in an announcement that the letters aim to put these companies on notice about deceptive or unfair marketing tactics that are likely unlawful. Activities in question include misrepresenting the benefits or limitations of a plan, or portraying a plan as comprehensive when it isn't.

In addition, FTC also warned against misrepresenting any costs associated with a plan or falsely telling consumers that a plan offers free rewards, cash offers or other incentives.

"Making healthcare more transparent and affordable is a top priority for the FTC," said Christopher Mufarrige, Director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, in the announcement.

"Americans experiencing rising healthcare costs should not also have to worry about whether a healthcare plan or program is what it claims to be," Mufarrige continued. "The FTC will remain focused on monitoring this market and will not hesitate to hold accountable companies that unlawfully market or advertise healthcare plans to consumers."

The FTC letters were largely sent to firms that market plans on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, where open enrollment opened on Sunday, Nov. 1. Medicare is also in its annual enrollment period, which continues through Dec. 7, and late fall is when most employers begin plan selections for workers.

The agency does not allege wrongdoing in the warning letters, but instead suggests that the companies "conduct a thorough review of their advertisements to ensure they are complying with applicable laws and rules."

The letters include examples of previous enforcement actions against marketers in the ACA space, such as Innovative Partners and Top Healthcare Options Insurance Agency.

In the letters, the agency emphasizes that its staff will be closely watching for potential violations.

"FTC staff will continue to actively monitor this market for potentially deceptive or unfair acts or practices and will take enforcement action as warranted," the FTC wrote in the letter (PDF).

#5675. The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure

New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.

The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.

Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.

Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.

To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.

Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.

To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.

The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.

After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.

Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.

Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits

After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.

These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.

By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.

The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.

By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.

Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.

Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade

The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.

Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.

This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.

However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.

"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.

"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."

Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5674. Is It Over for DAPT After Left Atrial Appendage Closure?

— Antithrombotic monotherapy worked at least as well at 6 months

Antithrombotic monotherapy was similar to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for 6-month outcomes after left atrial appendage (LAA) closure, the SIMPLAAFY trial showed.

The incidence rate of combined all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding at 6 months was 5.1% with reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs), 3.3% with aspirin alone, and 6.9% with DAPT, reported Saibal Kar, MD, of Los Robles Hospital and Medical Center in Thousand Oaks, California, at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

Statistically, the strategy of reduced-dose NOACs was at least as good as DAPT (risk ratio [RR] 0.75, 95% CI 0.48-1.18), as was aspirin alone (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.29-0.82).

"These findings support the simplification of antithrombotic management after uncomplicated LAA [closure] and may be individualized according to competing bleeding and device thrombosis risks and patient preferences," Kar said.

The study was simultaneously published in JAMA.

Among the secondary analyses in the trial, there was no excess stroke at 6 months with the aspirin or NOAC monotherapy regimens. However, bleeds alone gave both an edge over DAPT, while low-dose NOAC therapy stood out for a relatively low incidence of device-related thrombus (DRT) at 45 days (0.9% vs 3.4% with DAPT and 2.7% with aspirin).

As it stands, standard practice varies widely for antithrombotic therapy after LAA closure on account of a "lack of legitimate evidence" for guidance, said session discussant Mohamad Alkhouli, MD, of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota.

"Aspirin seems to emerge a winner," Alkhouli suggested, based on SIMPLAAFY, while he noted that "the jury is still out" for NOACs.

Complicating the picture is the ANDES trial, which found that after LAA closure, short-term NOACs were no better than DAPT at preventing DRT at 60 days, and were associated with even more DRTs at 1 year (5.2% vs 2.3%, P=0.154).

Kar said these data gave him pause on making a blanket recommendation for NOACs after LAA closure.

Meanwhile, 12-month results from SIMPLAAFY are still pending.

"The fact is that we really didn't know what to do with these patients," said Kar. "What we will do beyond 1 year, I don't know."

SIMPLAAFY included patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation who had the Watchman FLX Pro LAA occluder successfully implanted. The investigators randomized 1,857 patients 1:1:1 to aspirin 81 to 100 mg alone, initial DAPT for 6 months (followed by aspirin thereafter), or initial reduced-dose NOACs -- 2.5-mg apixaban (Eliquis) twice daily or 10-mg rivaroxaban (Xarelto) daily -- for 3 months (followed by aspirin thereafter).

Across the three study groups, mean age was 76 years, 43% were women, mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2, and mean HAS-BLED bleeding risk score was 2.6.

Acute events through 7 days were rare in general. Rates of clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding were 1.0% with aspirin alone, 1.6% with DAPT, and 1.5% with low-dose NOACs; major bleeding rates were 0.2%, 0.5%, and 0.2%, respectively.

The proportion of participants adhering to their assigned medications (for 80% or more days) was 87.9% with aspirin alone, 76.8% with DAPT, and 85.3% with reduced-dose NOACs. "Both monotherapy treatments were better tolerated than DAPT," Kar noted.

A subgroup analysis indicated that people ages 75 and older had disproportionately better outcomes on aspirin (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.18-0.64) or reduced-dose NOACs (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.31-0.93).

LAA imaging at 45 days suggested no differences in the Watchman device seal across groups.

Kar stressed that only uncomplicated LAA occluder implants were included in the trial, limiting the generalizability of the findings. Some high-risk populations were also excluded (e.g., those with severe kidney disease, recent stroke, myocardial infarction, or major bleeding).

Of note, there was no prespecified comparison of the two monotherapy arms.

#5673. LeanTaaS expands iQueue into ambient intelligence with LookDeep acquisition

LeanTaaS expands iQueue into ambient intelligence with LookDeep acquisition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare technology company LeanTaaS is expanding its iQueue platform beyond traditional hospital operations and capacity management into ambient intelligence, using computer vision to monitor patient rooms and turn signals into actions.

As part of this strategy, the company plans to launch iQueue for Virtual Care, using AI-powered patient-room monitoring to detect events such as fall risks, patient movement and other environmental signals, then route those insights into operational workflow.

The system is designed to turn events like an attempted bed exit into prioritized tasks rather than additional alarms. AI monitors rooms and surfaces events to a virtual observation team, which can assess the situation, remotely engage the patient or escalate to bedside staff when needed, Mohan Giridharadas, founder and CEO of LeanTaaS, told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Urgency and routing are based on the patient’s context and the health system’s established protocols. Human clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions, Giridharadas said, while iQueue provides context, prioritizes events and helps route information to the appropriate care team.

The company’s software and services are being used by nearly 200 health systems in more than 1,200 hospitals, centers and clinics in the U.S.

To accelerate this strategy, LeanTaaS acquired LookDeep Health, its second acquisition in about two months following its purchase of care transition platform Aidin. The deal brings computer vision technology, an open platform approach and virtual care deployment experience into LeanTaaS.

LeanTaaS provided Fierce Healthcare with a first look at the acquisition news. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

Giridharadas said the company is building the "central nervous system of the hospital," and computer vision will be a key data source for this broader hospital operations platform.

"It is a move beyond retrospective dashboards toward continuous operational awareness and execution," Giridharadas told Fierce Healthcare.

"A great operational brain needs more signal[s], so [that] it can decide faster and decide better. Health systems generate hundreds of thousands of data points each day—but the vast majority of them are discarded after they have served their immediate purpose. The next frontier is building a robust and scalable approach to capture high-value signals from the physical care environment that may never reach the EHR, or may reach it too late to be useful. That includes whether a patient is alone, trying to stand or hasn't been out of bed in days, when a nurse was last in the room, and whether a room is ready for the next patient, from compatible cameras and in-room devices, and potentially other device-generated or workflow signals," Giridharadas said.

"The test is whether a signal is sufficiently accurate and timely, and whether it can be converted into a clear action for the care team. We intend to continuously expand the sources and uses of data from the entire end-to-end patient journey," he added.

Narinder Singh, former CEO and co-founder of LookDeep who joined LeanTaaS as senior vice president of ambient intelligence, said the technology can support stretched care teams by monitoring patients when clinicians can’t be present. "Nurses and physicians cannot be in every room at every moment, and too often technology has added to their work instead of taking it away. Ambient intelligence keeps watch when they can't be there, so staff finally feel the technology works for them, not the other way around," he said in a statement.

LeanTaaS acquired LookDeep rather than partner with a computer vision or virtual care company to integrate ambient intelligence technology deeply into the iQueue platform, executives said.

"We are building the central nervous system of healthcare operations—a highly functional nervous system must have audio and video sensory capabilities in order to be effective. This is why we needed to acquire the capability rather than rely on an arms-length partnership. We already had the intelligence that drives the car, 15 years of it. What we wanted was the best perception ever built for hospitals. Nobody confuses the cameras with the car, but there is no self-driving car without them," Giridharadas said.

LookDeep brings three capabilities to LeanTaaS' platform: peer-reviewed vision AI, an open technology platform that works with hospitals’ existing infrastructure and experience deploying virtual care. Its approach also focuses on using AI to ease care team capacity constraints rather than adding to clinicians’ workloads.

Health systems can build on compatible cameras and in-room devices already in place or deploy supported hardware as needed. This open approach helps preserve existing investments while creating a foundation for new capabilities, according to the company.

"The acquisition gives us the opportunity to make ambient intelligence a native part of iQueue and extend the technology across our broader portfolio. We also share a conviction that in something as complex as a hospital, before you can be smart, you must be open. Vendor-specific camera silos will not last as health systems demand greater interoperability," Giridharadas said, noting that a camera alone "does not generate an ROI." "The value comes when what it sees changes what happens next—earlier, with the right person acting. Nobody expects the barcode scanner to redefine the supply chain, yet no supply chain runs well without one."

The new virtual care offering includes three services: virtual observation for AI-assisted patient monitoring and escalation, virtual nursing to support admissions, rounding, patient education and discharge preparation, and virtual medicine to connect patients with remote physicians and specialists.

These offerings build on LookDeep’s experience deploying the technology in health systems. Across different deployments and operating models, reported results include a more than 70% reduction in fall rates, twice as much nursing contact, an 80% reduction in medication errors and threefold cost savings compared with traditional virtual sitting solutions, according to the companies.

Beyond virtual care, LeanTaaS plans to incorporate ambient intelligence into additional iQueue products and workflows to support capacity, patient flow and care coordination.

"We will bring the vision capability into all of our products beginning with inpatient flow and operating rooms and then moving on to infusion centers and other areas of the hospital," Giridharadas said.

The company aims to find areas in hospital patient care where important signals are either missed or received too late by current systems. "We will prioritize use cases where the signal is reliable, the response is well defined and the impact can be measured," he noted.

As adoption of AI in healthcare grows, LeanTaaS says its competitive advantage comes from a proprietary knowledge base built from more than 15 years of health system deployments. "We have accumulated an enormous knowledge base of thousands of corner cases that make operational improvement and change management difficult to accomplish. We have built a multi-layered knowledge architecture of tens of thousands of 'knowledge nodes' that enables us to deliver an enterprise-grade AI capability where the data and knowledge is tightly curated to the unique needs of each site at each customer rather than relying on generic recommendations from foundation LLM models," he said.

#5672. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.
