#5575. Google fine-tunes its Agentic Data Cloud to support highly scalable autonomous AI workers

Artificial intelligence is no longer just about conversational assistants that tell people what to do. These days, it’s all about work automation, and Google Cloud is making sure it’s right at the forefront of that trend with its revamped Agentic Data Cloud platform, which received a host of new updates today.

The Agentic Data Cloud was launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next. It’s meant to be the architectural “system of action” for AI agents, replacing the brittle extract, transform and load-based data pipelines, or ETL, that feed legacy software applications. The key advantage of Agentic Data Cloud is that it meets customers where their data is, so rather than forcing them to squeeze all of their information in a large, centralized data warehouse, it enables AI agents to access it wherever it lives.

In a blog post, Sirish Chandrasekaran, Google’s vice president of product management for data analytics, outlined the company’s belief that autonomous agents rather than humans will soon become the primary consumers of data. As such, it makes sense to build a purpose-built infrastructure stack specifically for them, prioritizing low latency, zero data movement and automated governance. “That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a system of action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost,” Chandrasekaran said.

The flagship new feature in Agentic Data Cloud is borderless Lakehouse, a special version of Google’s “cross-border Lakehouse” product that also debuted at Cloud Next. Chandrasekaran said borderless Lakehouse is built upon the open-source Apache Iceberg table format and designed to eliminate multicloud friction with new caching capabilities for Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. This allows companies to query remote data held in those cloud platforms over a secure private link, without having to pay egress fees.

Chandrasekaran detailed how it works, saying that it automatically caches retrieved data blocks within Google Cloud to accelerate subsequent queries. There’s also a new AlloyDB integration that allows users to query external Iceberg tables with standard PostgreSQL queries without having to copy data. In this way, it bridges real-time transactional data with historical lakehouse records.

One of the big problems with autonomous agents is that they can be prone to hallucinations without proper guardrails in place, which is why Google has overhauled another capability within Agentic Data Cloud. The Knowledge Catalog, which is a kind of map of business meaning that’s meant to inform AI agents of the peculiarities of the organization they work for, is getting a new self-learning enrichment capability in preview.

According to Chandrasekaran, it works by continuously scanning unstructured data in Google Workspace, Jira, SharePoint and GitHub to translate operational knowledge into Open Knowledge Format context sets. These can be used to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge, and the results from early adopters shows that it can help make the average agent four-times more accurate, while reducing token consumption by up to 75%.

Knowledge Catalog is seen as so important to Google’s agentic future that it’s also being enabled by default in the Gemini application starting today. Because it’s so tightly integrated, it can resolve issues around business metric definitions and access controls before it translates user’s prompts into Structured Query Language queries. Companies can also choose to ground agents in semantic models for specific data platforms, including Google BigQuery, Snowflake, SAP, Looker and dbt.

“Agents are only as accurate as the business context they’re grounded in,” Chandrasekaran said. “Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on.”

Gemini is also getting new autonomous machine learning capabilities that can help to streamline everyday work for both technical teams and business workers. For instance, data engineers can now tell Gemini a specific business outcome they want to achieve in natural language, and Gemini will generate the PySpark code, run the notebooks and fix any data pipeline errors as it works toward that goal. Meanwhile, business users will be able to generate reliable, real-time operational reports in Gemini simply by asking for them.

“Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query,” Chandrasekaran explained. “Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent and verified answers every time.”

Google also has a few gifts for software developers, starting with the new Data Agent Kit, which is generally available from today, bringing Model Context Protocol tooling into integrated development environments such as VS Code, Claude Code and Antigravity. This means that developers can now just define their business intent in natural language and have agents automatically create, fine-tune and test the associated data pipelines.

Developers can also take advantage of infrastructure updates that are designed to facilitate “high-concurrency agent interactions,” so that thousands of AI agents can query the same database simultaneously without swamping it and causing problems. These include the broader preview of AlloyDB Express, a highly scalable database that supports sub-two-second provisioning for rapid agent prototyping. There’s also PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, which provides an isolated workload environment that can handle three million queries per second.

Finally, Google said BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics into relational database tables with zero ETL. It’s joined by previews of the TimesFM 3.0 forecasting model and TabFM predictive analytics model.

#5574. Tennessee Voters Opt To Ban State-Level Property Taxes

Voters in Tennessee are projected to approve Amendment 2, which bans any future statewide property tax and enshrines the prohibition in the state constitution.

Tennessee has not had a statewide property tax since 1949, though the state Legislature technically retained the constitutional authority to create one. Instead, property taxes are levied at the local level.

At 11 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the measure had 66.4% support with 82% of votes reporting, according to The Associated Press. An amendment to the Tennessee Constitution passes if it gets at least 50% support, and the number of “yes” votes is more than half of all votes cast for governor.

"It ensures that the state cannot impose property taxes again, putting taxpayers’ interests first and reinforcing local control," said Republican state Rep. Tandy Darby, who sponsored the amendment.

Amendment 2 would not prevent counties and municipal authorities from levying property taxes, but would prohibit the General Assembly from issuing property taxes now and in the future.

In order to change that, the state constitution would have to be amended once more, which would require a two-thirds vote in two legislative sessions and voter approval.

Republican Gov. Bill Lee came out in support of the initiative. It's supported by the National Federation of Independent Business as well as the Tennessee Realtors®.

Conservative nonprofit Tennessee Stands said the amendment "reinforces the principle that private property rights should never be subject to excessive government taxation or the threat of confiscation."

Some Democrats have opposed it on the grounds that the ban does not need to be written into the constitution and should remain a state statute.

#5573. The Home Depot Foundation Expands Veteran Housing Commitment to $1 Billion

The Home Depot Foundation is increasing its total commitment to veteran causes to $1 billion through 2032, expanding investments in programs designed to address veteran homelessness, housing insecurity, and home accessibility.

Since 2011, the foundation says it has invested more than $650 million in veteran causes and helped improve more than 70,000 veteran homes and facilities. Its latest commitment will combine established housing programs with efforts to test and scale new approaches to veteran housing.

“We believe every veteran deserves a safe place to call home,” said Erin Izen, executive director of The Home Depot Foundation. “Our $1 billion commitment supports the partnerships and solutions needed to help more veterans move from uncertainty to long-term stability.”

Among the initiatives receiving support are programs designed to remove barriers to rental housing. The Landlords, Organizations, and Veterans Engagement (LOVE) Fund, with Open Doors Atlanta, and the U.S. VETS Master Lease Program aim to speed veteran housing placements by addressing costs such as security deposits and application fees or by leasing units directly from property owners.

The foundation is also investing in homelessness prevention and permanent supportive housing through organizations including Operation Homefront and Community Solutions. Additional funding will explore alternative housing approaches, including modular homes from Purple Heart Homes for senior veterans and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The announcement coincides with the foundation’s annual Celebration of Service. This fall, Team Depot, The Home Depot’s associate volunteer force, is expected to complete hundreds of projects benefiting veterans across all 50 states and three U.S. territories.

One recent project brought The Home Depot Foundation, Team Depot, and Purple Heart Homes together to construct a fully accessible modular home on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for James “Jim” Taylor, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who previously experienced homelessness. The home was subsequently transported to Virginia, where a dedication is planned.

#5572. LGI Homes Posts Q3 Gains Despite Slower Sales Activity

LGI Homes posted year-over-year gains in closings, revenue, and earnings during the third quarter, even as affordability pressures continued to weigh on buyer demand and slow sales activity.

The Texas-based builder delivered 1,222 homes during the quarter, up 10.4% from a year earlier, including 33 currently and previously leased homes. Its 1,189 new-home closings generated $437.5 million in home building revenue, an increase of 10.3% year over year. Total revenue increased 10.2% to $444.5 million.

“We delivered strong third quarter financial results, generating year-over-year growth in closings, revenue, and earnings while maintaining strong profitability, expanding our community count, and further strengthening our balance sheet,” chairman and CEO Eric Lipar said.

Net income increased to $24.6 million from $19.7 million in the prior-year quarter, while diluted earnings per share increased to $1.05 from $0.85.

Home building gross margin was 20.2% in the third quarter, while adjusted home building gross margin was 23.7%. Both were above the midpoint of LGI Homes’ previous guidance ranges and improved 40 basis points sequentially.

Lipar attributed the margin performance in part to the company’s predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet land position and its approach to balancing affordability and profitability.

“Our teams also did an excellent job managing costs. SG&A expenses declined on an absolute-dollar basis, and SG&A as a percentage of total revenues improved 180 basis points year over year,” he said.

The builder also continued expanding its footprint, ending the third quarter with 151 active communities, an increase of 7.1% from the prior-year period.

Despite stronger closings and revenue, LGI Homes said affordability pressure contributed to slower sales activity during the quarter.

Through the first nine months of 2026, net orders totaled 2,869, compared with 4,098 during the same period in 2025. The cancellation rate increased to 48.9% from 28.1%, while ending backlog declined to 685 homes from 1,305 a year earlier.

The trend marks a reversal from the beginning of the year, when LGI Homes ended the first quarter with 1,699 homes in backlog, up 63.4% year over year. At the time, management pointed to improving sales activity and a growing backlog as evidence of steady demand heading into the spring selling season.

By the third quarter, however, affordability had become a more significant headwind.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership and are leaning into our proven sales and marketing strategies to improve sales pace while maintaining our disciplined approach to balancing affordability and profitability,” Lipar said.

Based on its year-to-date results and current market conditions, LGI Homes narrowed its full-year closing guidance and now expects to deliver between 4,600 and 4,800 homes in 2026. The company said the revised outlook reflects slower sales activity as affordability pressures continue to weigh on demand.

The builder maintained the remainder of its full-year guidance, including an expected average sales price between $360,000 and $370,000 and adjusted home building gross margin between 22.5% and 24.5%.

“As we head into the final quarter of the year, our focus is on finishing 2026 strong,” Lipar said. “Affordability remains the key consideration for today’s buyers, and we have intentionally broadened our sales process to work with more prospective customers who may need additional time to qualify.”

In the 2026 elections, voters decided all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats, and numerous housing-related measures. Both Democrats and Republicans have listed priorities to improve housing affordability in coming years.

"Tonight’s Democratic sweep shuffles control of the legislative branch, but the economic impact, which is fundamental for the U.S. housing market, is far less clear," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel. "Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen."

Housing issues have been a dominant note in 2026, as Americans struggle with affordability. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hit its highest level in three years last month before dipping back to 7.24% last week, according to Fannie Mae. The national average gas price is $4.14 a gallon compared to $3.03 a year ago, according to AAA. President Donald Trump has pledged to focus on affordability issues.

"President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Realtor.com in a statement on Tuesday morning.

Ingle noted that Trump in his second term had signed an executive order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and "cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs."

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," he said.

Congress passed a bipartisan housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, this summer. But it will take years for some of those changes to take effect in the market. And lawmakers expect states and local governments to implement some changes.

The Trump administration, meantime, has undertaken other changes such as encouraging more innovation in the homebuilding sector and reducing rules for some housing, like manufactured homes. It's also sought to limit the impact of institutional investors in the housing market.

"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump posted on X late Tuesday, as major news outlets projected Democrats would take control of the House after flipping a half-dozen seats. Trump later told The New York Times he would accept the results of the election.

The economist Krimmel says that one "wild card" to keep an eye on is how the election outcome affects Trump's war with Iran.

"Many Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, which has sparked inflationary oil supply shortages," he says. "A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates. However, a lot of uncertainty remains. Wanting the conflict to end and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things."

Democrats marked the evening with several key wins in both the House and the Senate.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews flipped the Senate seat formerly held by Republican Lindsey Graham. Andrews beat Graham's sister, Darlene Graham, who had been picked by Trump.

And Democrat James Talarico flipped a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat in almost a century to be elected to the Senate.

Democrats had several early victories. Democratic former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper flipped the state's Senate seat, replacing Republican Thom Tillis, who chairs the Senate's Financial Institutions and Consumer Protection Subcommittee. Democrat Jamie Ager also flipped a North Carolina House district.

"We knew that the chaos and corruption in Washington were hurting our people," Cooper said in a speech. "Today, you said, 'This has to stop.'"

Pennsylvania saw three formerly Republican seats picked up by Democrats Janelle Stelson, Paige Cognetti, and Bob Brooks. They ousted incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan Jr., and Scott Perry.

In New Jersey, Tom Kean Jr. lost reelection after an extended absence fueled national headlines. Meanwhile, in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown returned to Congress after campaigning heavily against incumbent Jon Husted, attacking the Republication over his prior support of data centers.

"Politics should never, ever be about two private clubs who are more interested in beating up each other than they are in solving problems," said Josh Turek, who flipped a Senate seat in Iowa for Democrats.

On Truth Social, Trump posted a photo of a red hat with the word "veto." He has repeatedly criticized Democrats this year saying their policies drive up housing and other costs.

Trump told Fox News late on Tuesday night that he would not shy away from using presidential vetoes to block "crazy" measures advanced by Democrats in Congress.

"I have the power of veto, and the power of veto, you know, it's impervious," the president said.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, who won reelection in Louisiana, defended Republicans' economic actions in remarks before midnight. He said Americans would "suffer" if Democrats use control of Congress to enact "retribution" over the next two years.

"From the first day of this election we knew that to keep the House and sustain the majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said. "It's very, very difficult to overcome."

But Johnson said an agenda of "common sense" would lead Republicans to take back the House in 2028.

"Republicans have much more work to do," he said. "The new Congress doesn't change that at all."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5569. Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer now builds AI agents and retrains the models behind them

Enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Oumi PBC today extended its Frontier AI Engineer agent so it can build AI agents for customers and retrain the models those agents run on.

The release goes after a problem that tends to surface once agents leave the demo stage. A failing agent might have a bad prompt, a broken tool or a weak underlying model.

Oumi says enterprises have traditionally tried to fix it with prompt and harness engineering because retraining a model’s weights has required skills normally found at frontier AI labs. That approach often stalls before the agent is reliable enough to put to work.

Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer already sets objectives, designs evaluations and runs training experiments for custom models on its platform. With today’s update, a team can describe in plain language what it wants an agent to accomplish, and FAiE helps define the tools and environments that agent needs before moving on to evaluation and training. Whatever goes wrong once the agent is in production is turned into evaluation sets and training data for the next round.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Manos Koukoumidis said better prompts and bigger generic models will only take agents so far. The ones that succeed will improve “by training the weights of the models powering them, learning from their own work,” he said, pointing to failed tasks and user preferences as the signals that count.

Companies that already run agents elsewhere can keep them there. Under a feature Oumi calls Bring Your Own Harness, the customer’s orchestration, tools and memory stay put and connect to Oumi for evaluation and model training. Models end up tuned in the same environment the agent works in every day.

Oumi is also adding direct preference optimization to the supervised fine-tuning it already supported, so a model can be trained on examples of the behavior users preferred. Reinforcement learning arrives through group relative policy optimization, which grades a model on task outcomes. Several methods can be chained together in a single multistage training run, and FAiE helps choose the strategy, set up rewards and diagnose problems along the way.

The training work feeds Oumi’s broader argument about model ownership. Most enterprise agents run on general-purpose models from frontier AI providers that aren’t optimized for a particular customer’s work. The company’s pitch since launching a commercial platform for custom models in March has been that a specialized model the customer owns outright can do better work at lower cost.

Group relative policy optimization is launching in private preview, and the Seattle company is taking requests for access. Oumi is a venture capital-backed startup that raised a $10 million seed round led by Venrock Management and Obvious Management Services in January 2025. The founding team includes former engineering leaders from Google LLC’s Gemini group.

Paul Breunich, executive chairman of William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, announced that Carolyn Fugere has been appointed president and Chief Executive Officer.

According to a release, Fugere will lead the real estate company serving Connecticut, Westchester County and the Hudson Valley in New York, and the Berkshires in Massachusetts.

During her service as co-president and chief sales officer—where she was responsible for overseeing 31 offices and 1,100 sales advisors—the company posted the highest total closed dollar volume for any five-year period in the company’s history, the release states.

Fugere will become the fourth CEO in the company’s 77-year history, and the first-ever woman to hold the position. The release notes that in 2026, William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty rose to the rank of the top-producing, independently-owned Sotheby’s International Realty affiliate by sales volume and closed units worldwide for the global brand, which encompasses nearly 1,075 offices throughout 81 countries and territories on six continents.

Fugere commented that this No. 1 ranking serves as an opportunity and a responsibility to continue raising the standard of professional real estate advisory services.

“I’ve always believed that the measure of our success is the positive impact we have on the people around us,” Fugere said. “Whether we’re helping our advisors grow, supporting our colleagues, guiding our clients through important moments in their lives, or contributing to the communities we serve, we have an opportunity every day to make a difference. We have an extraordinary organization, and I believe we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to continue raising the standard of our profession.”

Fugere’s tenure in residential real estate spans 25 years in total and 16 with William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, where she has grown in her career through multiple roles.

She embarked in the industry as a sales advisor, marketing and selling in suburban, urban and rural markets, and then advanced into brokerage management, leading eight sales offices across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York.

Fugere was honored twice as a Manager of the Year, and she oversaw the firm’s expansion in a brand-new territory in the Berkshires. She also restructured and headed the company’s training department, leading training initiatives for agents and staff before stepping into the co-president role.

From his initial recruitment meeting with Fugere in her days as a brokerage manager with her prior firm, Breunich recalled recognizing her talent.

“I told her she could stay at her old company and be a soldier, or she could come to our company and become a generaI. I got the general,” he said.

“Rather than a change in direction, this appointment is an exciting evolution in the leadership of our firm, and a natural progression of Carolyn’s work and commitment to the organization,” Breunich added. “She has been deeply involved in shaping the company’s culture, vision and strategy for many years.”

“Real estate is more than a profession to me. It is a lifelong passion centered entirely on the success of our agents,” Fugere said. “I am honored to step into this role and lead an organization I care so deeply about. Backed by an extraordinary team, my focus remains on supporting our advisors, strengthening the relationships that drive our business and continuing to build on what makes our organization so special.”

#5566. Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet

The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump.

Two key metrics—price cuts and delistings—tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall.

Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday.

On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning.

According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel, delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress.

However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet.

"Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson, a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing."

The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts.

According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated.

For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record.

However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points.

Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak, an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA, tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages."

Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market.

"Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress."

Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each.

Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September.

At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%).

While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback.

New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years.

"Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel.

At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023.

However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October.

For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September.

"Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas."

However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened.

"Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions."

Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee, and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers.

Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty.

"No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5565. EXCLUSIVE: Food Network Star Alex Guarnaschelli Reveals Her Secrets To Turning Any Home Into a Holiday Entertaining Hub

Turning your home into a welcoming holiday gathering spot doesn’t have to mean buying new decorations or finding room for a formal dining setup.

For Alex Guarnaschelli, a few thoughtful touches—and some planning before the doorbell rings—can help hosts make the most of their space and enjoy the celebration themselves.

In an exclusive interview with Realtor.com®, the celebrity chef shared her advice for entertaining on a budget, organizing a busy kitchen, and keeping guests comfortable in smaller homes.

“I always think a welcoming home is about the little details, not how much money you spend," she said.Her first suggestion is to adjust the lighting before guests arrive.

"A few candles or lamps instead of bright overhead lighting can completely change the feeling of a room," she explained.

When it comes to decorations, Guarnaschelli recommends looking for items that can serve another purpose once the party ends.

“Second, bring something natural into the space," she said. "I love the idea of filling a bowl with beautiful oranges, pomegranates, or even fresh herbs from the grocery store. They're inexpensive, they look festive, and you can actually use them afterward.”

Making guests comfortable from the moment they enter is another priority.

“And third, think about what your guests experience when they arrive. Have a place for coats and bags, put on some music, and make sure there's something to eat or drink right away,” she advised.

“You don't need a house that looks like a magazine. You just want people to walk in and feel like they're in the right place.”

That thoughtful approach extends to the kitchen, where Guarnaschelli starts by considering how each dish fits into the cooking schedule.

“I like to think of my kitchen almost like a restaurant kitchen before service. Everything should have a purpose and a place,” she explained. “I start by looking at what I'm making and working backward. What needs the oven? What needs the stove? What can stay in the refrigerator until the last minute? You don't want three dishes competing for the same burner when everyone's ready to eat.”

She also recommends deciding how food will be presented before it is ready to leave the kitchen.

“I also pull out the serving dishes ahead of time and decide what goes where. Sometimes I'll even put a little note in each platter so I don't have to think about it later. And clear your counters!” she added.

Choosing equipment that handles several tasks can also help keep the cooking area manageable.

Guarnaschelli points to a piece from her new HSN collection as an example.

“That's also why I love versatile tools, like the sauté pan from my new HSN collection. You can use it for everything from searing chicken to sautéing vegetables or making a quick sauce, without having to pull out a different pan for every dish,” she says. “A little organization and the right tools can make the whole evening feel easier.”

For those entertaining in an apartment or smaller home, Guarnaschelli suggests spreading refreshments across different areas to prevent guests from gathering around the stove.

“The trick to entertaining in a small space is to give people a reason to spread out. If you put the drinks, appetizers, and main course all next to the stove, you're going to end up with a crowd exactly where you’re cooking!”

A side table can become a drink station, while appetizers can encourage guests to mingle elsewhere.

“I would put drinks in the living room, maybe on a bar cart or even a cleared-off side table, and keep a few appetizers somewhere else. A cheese board is great because people can help themselves without needing you to do anything,” she explained.

Guarnaschelli also recommends making use of vertical space when arranging the food.

“I also love using different heights when setting out food. A cake stand or a raised platter can give you more room without taking over the entire table," she added.

And hosts needn’t feel pressured to create a traditional seated dinner.

“Don't feel like everyone needs a formal seat at the same time. Sometimes a more relaxed, casual setup makes for the best party," the chef noted.

Preparing ahead can further reduce the number of tasks competing for a host’s attention. For Guarnaschelli, the day before a gathering is an opportunity to work through smaller jobs.

“The day before a party is when I like to tackle all the little jobs that have a way of piling up. Wash your herbs, measure out ingredients, make your salad dressing, and get your serving dishes ready.”

She also uses equipment from her collection to help with ingredient preparation.

“This is also where a tool like the cordless chopper from my new HSN collection really comes in handy," she added. "You can get through chopping onions, herbs, and other ingredients for your recipes without spending the entire afternoon doing prep work.”

Depending on the menu, some cooking can be completed ahead of time, too.

“You can even prepare things like a soup or a braised dish that will taste better the next day because the flavors have had time to come together," the food guru revealed.

Before filling the kitchen with prepared dishes, however, Guarnaschelli recommended checking that there is somewhere to store them.

“I also like to make sure the refrigerator has enough room for everything before I start cooking. That's one of those things nobody thinks about until they're trying to squeeze a giant platter onto a shelf that's already full.”

On the day of the gathering, she focuses on dishes that need to be finished close to serving.

“For the day of, save the things that really need your attention, like roasting meat, crisping up potatoes, or finishing vegetables. Anything that needs to be hot and fresh should get that last bit of care," the chef said.

Her final suggestion is to leave enough time to welcome guests without simultaneously scrambling to finish the meal.

“Give yourself a little buffer before guests arrive," she said. "You don't want to be pulling something out of the oven with one hand while answering the door with the other.”

#5564. Descope launches Envoy to let consumer apps accept personal AI agents as users

Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today launched Envoy, a service that lets consumer websites and apps accept personal artificial intelligence agents acting for their customers without rebuilding how people sign in.

Agents arriving through Envoy get an identity of their own, separate from the customer’s. The launch goes after a choice consumer businesses have been stuck with since agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse started shopping and paying for things on people’s behalf.

Amazon.com Inc. blocked Muse from its store in September, saying the agent did not identify itself as one when placing orders, and JPMorgan Chase & Co. moved a month later to keep outside agents away from customer bank accounts. Descope expects blocking will get harder to maintain as more customers do their shopping through an agent.

The alternative, in Descope’s telling, is an agent that signs in as the customer with the person’s own password and one-time code. Nothing in that session shows software was involved, so when a fraud rule fires the logs point at the person. The business ends up absorbing the cost in disputed orders and returns.

Envoy is built around a proposed standard that offers a third option. Meta and Sierra Technologies Inc. published a 0.1 draft of the Personal Agent Protocol in October to set rules for how an agent signs in for someone without posing as them. Under Poppy, as the draft is known, a business publishes the endpoints agents should use and verifies which agent is calling. The business then issues a session bound cryptographically to that agent until the interaction ends.

Developers who adopt Envoy do not have to implement Poppy themselves or keep pace with revisions to it. Descope runs discovery and agent identification, and agents need no advance registration because each one presents a published client metadata document. Session tokens are tied to a key the agent holds through the Demonstrating Proof of Possession standard. Envoy supports all three of the draft’s sign-in types.

Inside Envoy, businesses spell out what an agent is allowed to do on a customer’s account through the Rich Authorization Requests extension to OAuth. In the example Descope gives, a retailer could let a shopping agent place orders for a customer and still keep it away from the payment methods on file. How long any elevated access lasts is left to the retailer as well.

Sensitive actions can go back to the customer for approval on a separate channel, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication. Another example from Descope has an agent booking travel hold a fare it found overnight and send the details to the customer’s phone for approval the next morning.

Every token and log entry records the customer and the agent as separate parties, so a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out. Envoy runs alongside whatever customer identity system a business already has.

Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said every login page on the internet was built for a person on the other side, and “that assumption no longer holds true.” In his view, the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what the Model Context Protocol did for enterprise tools.

GoFundMe Inc. and GoodRx Holdings Inc. are among the launch and design partners working with Descope on Envoy over the coming months. Each donation on GoFundMe is “an act of trust,” according to Arnie Katz, the fundraising platform’s chief product and technology officer. He said Envoy will keep the donor and the agent distinct in every session and ask users to approve donations from their phones.

At GoodRx, Chief Technology Officer Nitin Shingate expects people to send agents out to compare pharmacies and find the lowest price on a prescription before they reach the counter. Agents there will get limited permissions covering pricing information.

Agent builders get a tool of their own. A Poppy software development kit, released alongside Envoy, lets any agent work with the protocol, with Descope handling discovery and session management behind it. The kit is written in TypeScript and has no external dependencies.

Envoy sits on top of Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub, which the company updated last month with controls aimed at agents employees build or adopt inside their own organizations. The hub now handles authentication and access control for more than 1,000 MCP servers and millions of agent transactions each month, according to Descope.

Descope is a venture capital-backed startup whose investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Notable Capital and Dell Technologies Capital. The company has raised $88 million to date, including a $35 million seed extension in September 2025.

#5563. This 83-Acre Blue Ridge Mountain Wedding Estate Is Heading to Auction With No Reserve

Imagine hosting a wedding or lavish event for 150 friends and family right on your very own Blue Ridge Mountain farm.

That could become a reality as an 83.56-acre property with a 5,000-square-foot event barn in Franklin, NC, heads to auction with no reserve on Nov. 7.

Created in 2010, Tessentee Farm has multiple structures, including an eight-bedroom primary residence, three two-bedroom guest cabins, and plenty of space to entertain.

"It has a nice big spread of land, so the duality of it also being an income-generating asset is pretty impressive," says Trayor Lesnock, founder and president of Platinum Luxury Auctions, who will host the auction. The listing is held by Isaiah Thomas Johns of Mountain Pro Real Estate Professionals.

The property last changed hands for $2,500,000 in 2013 and had hit the market for $6.9 million in November 2025.

“You have this large house with all the bells and whistles where you could live, an event barn, and three separate cabins where you could host events,” Lesnock says. “There is a good record of the farm being used for weddings and events.”

The luxury event barn, which can be heated and cooled, has hosted everything from destination weddings and rehearsal dinners to milestone celebrations and corporate retreats.

“We have had large families from the Blue Ridge Mountain region look at it and are wanting to use it for multigenerational living,” he notes. “About 50% were looking to use it as a private property and the other 50% were looking at it for the income generation.”

The primary residence has arched doorways, built-ins, French doors, a spacious dining room, a chef's kitchen with a breakfast bar, and a primary suite with a fireplace, soaking tub, and walk-in shower.

Covered terraces overlook the pool, which has a water slide and a swim-up bar, as well as an outdoor kitchen and a hot tub.

“It will probably go to someone who wants to use it privately,” Lesnock adds. “There are no outright restrictions, so you could develop it further.”

The rustic barn has exposed beams, wood-paneled walls, string lighting, and an open field ideal for photos. A ceremony could be held in the pasture, followed by cocktails under the stars, and dinner and dancing inside the barn, with guests retreating to cabins for an overnight stay.

Lesnock says the countryside setting could lend itself to an equestrian estate.

“You could make it more of a farm and add an arena if you wanted,” he says. “Franklin is not an area that pops up on a lot of people’s maps, but it’s in the southern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville is only an hour away. There is also a creek that borders the property that is excellent for trout fishing.”

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. #5562. Tether Bitcoin Holdings Rival Corporate Treasury Giants

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Tether Bitcoin holdings have reached 150,000 BTC, putting the company behind USDT among the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holders.

CEO Paolo Ardoino revealed the figure during his keynote at the Plan ₿ Forum in Lugano, Switzerland, on November 3. The position is worth $11.5 billion at the current price.

🔥BIG: Tether holds about 150,000 BTC worth $11.5 BILLION, CEO Paolo Ardoino reveals.That tops every public company on BitcoinTreasuries’ list except Strategy, which holds 849,327 BTC, about 5.7 times as much.Privately held Tether sits outside the ranking.The figure is… pic.twitter.com/bDdTZ1G3DW

The disclosure places Tether behind only Strategy among major corporate Bitcoin treasury holders. It also highlights how the stablecoin giant is turning profits from its dollar-pegged business into a substantial Bitcoin position.

Tether has built its treasury through a strategy announced in May 2023. The company committed to allocating up to 15% of its net realized operating profits toward Bitcoin purchases.

Tether’s estimated 150,000 BTC position puts it well ahead of most companies pursuing Bitcoin treasury strategies. Strategy remains the clear leader, holding 849,327 BTC. Tether’s reported stack represents 18% of Strategy’s holdings, placing the stablecoin issuer among the industry’s largest corporate Bitcoin buyers.

The disclosure also puts Tether ahead of companies such as Metaplanet and Strive, whose Bitcoin treasuries remain below 50,000 BTC each.

Ardoino discussed the holdings while outlining Tether’s expanding role in the Bitcoin ecosystem. He also said the company serves more than 730 million users worldwide, adding 30 million wallets each quarter.

Tether’s Bitcoin strategy began in 2023, when the company announced plans to invest a portion of its operating profits into BTC. The policy allows Tether to accumulate Bitcoin using earnings from its business rather than relying entirely on external fundraising.

The company has also invested in gold, energy, Bitcoin mining infrastructure, and other technology projects. Bitcoin remains one of its most prominent long-term investment positions.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Tether’s growing Bitcoin holdings are backed by a highly profitable stablecoin business. The company generated $4.5 billion in net operating profit during the first nine months of 2026, including $1.5 billion in the third quarter.

USDT issuance remained near $184 billion during the period, while Treasury bills and reverse repurchase agreements continued generating most of Tether’s income.

Tether’s third-quarter attestation showed $191.45 billion in reserve assets against $183.50 billion in liabilities. Its excess reserves climbed to $7.95 billion, nearly doubling from $4.1 billion at the end of June.

The company also reported $132.4 billion in direct and indirect US Treasury bill exposure, giving it a substantial source of recurring income.

This business model separates Tether from companies that raise capital specifically to buy Bitcoin. Strategy has relied heavily on stock sales and debt offerings to expand its treasury, while Tether can allocate a portion of its operating profits toward BTC.

Tether latest disclosure also puts its Bitcoin holdings above the amount listed in its third-quarter USDT reserve report. That report valued Bitcoin reserves at $8.37 billion on September 30, while Ardoino’s estimate puts the company’s total position near $11.5 billion.

Tether’s growing Bitcoin treasury shows how stablecoin profits can fund a major corporate crypto position. With USDT remaining one of the industry’s largest dollar-backed tokens, the company has a recurring earnings engine supporting its long-term Bitcoin strategy.

Strategy still holds a much larger stack, but Tether has emerged as a powerful corporate Bitcoin holder in its own right.

#5561. Mortgage Rates Continue To Fall, but Purchase Applications Retreat

Mortgage applications fell last week, even as interest rates on home loans declined for the third week in a row, giving buyers some relief.

For the week ending Oct. 30 the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—decreased 1.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, decreased 2% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment. Purchase applications were down 19% from a year ago.

According to MBA calculations, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances is 7.3%, a slight decrease from last week's rate of 7.37%. Rates averaged 6.17% a year ago.

Mortgage rates dropped to 7.24% last week from 7.32% the week before, according to a separate survey from Freddie Mac.

"Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting,” said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s SVP and Chief Economist. “While the 30-year rate declined to 7.3%, activity is still quite slow, with purchase application volume down for the week and refinance volume effectively flat at a very low level."

As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025.”

That's pushed more borrowers to pursue riskier adjustable-rate mortgages. According to Fratantoni, the share of ARM applications is at its highest level since September 2025.

ARM rates are nearly a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, and the share of ARM applications increased week over week from 11.3% to 11.4%.

The share of FHA loan applications decreased to 16% from 16.6% the prior week. The VA share of total applications increased to 11.2% from 11% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications increased to 0.6% from 0.5% the week prior.

Meanwhile, the refinance share of mortgage activity increased to 39.8% from 38.9% the previous week. Though the overall refinance index increased .1% from the previous week, it was 60% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked into their lower interest rates.

While Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee opted not to raise rates again last week, rate watchers are looking ahead to December when the Fed meets again to decide on rates.

CME Group's FedWatch has the likelihood of an additional rate hike at just under 80%.

With Democrats wresting control of the House and Senate on Tuesday, voters will be watching to see what economic policies are instituted to help make housing more affordable.

"Many Democrat campaigns tapped into voter dissatisfaction with the economy, a winning strategy in 2026. Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel.

"Legislative options are likely to be limited in a divided Washington where a Democratic House and Senate will either need to work with the Republican White House or find enough Republican legislative support to override a likely veto," he adds.

Mortgage rates are calculated based on various factors in the economy, and the length of your loan and credit score will also factor into the mortgage rate you qualify for.

The 30-year mortgage rate is tied to the yield of the 10-year Treasury note, because most 30-year mortgages are either paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

Long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

#5560. Tencent releases Hy4, a powerful frontier AI model introducing visual understanding and computer use

Tencent Holdings Ltd. today introduced Hy4, a new large language model that adds computer-use capabilities for the first time, using advanced visual understanding, reasoning and tool-calling to deliver long-horizon agentic performance.

The company said the model marks a significant leap in performance over its Hy4 Preview, which arrived Aug. 28, weighing in at 770 billion parameters with 49 billion active parameters. Both provide a 1 million-token context window, putting it in the same range as current open-weights frontier models from European and Chinese developers, including Mistral AI SAS, Beijing Moonshot Technology Co. Ltd. and Z.AI Co. Ltd.

The company said it substantially scaled up both pre-training and post-training, reporting gains over the preview version in instruction following, long-context understanding, agentic long-horizon tasks and deep research. Tencent also identified excessive reasoning and over-verification during the previous version’s “thinking” processes.

The new model focuses heavily on real-world productivity for workplace collaboration, human experience and professional work. The company said it optimized long-context learning capabilities to understand complex information, including web development, document summarization, visual creative tasks, document presentation, and more.

The company added that it also enhanced its capability for front-end and game development, high-complexity tasks that include intricate business logic, state management and orchestration. Some models struggle with producing stateful, elegant and beautiful user interfaces that are visually polished and also fully functional.

It is not uncommon for professional game developers, industry engineers and amateur vibe coders to use AI models as part of their work. However, a recent spate has had coders begin to reproduce, reverse-engineer and clone older and semi-recent video games. That prompted Anthropic PBC to block Claude Code and its underlying Opus 5.5 model from assisting in these tasks.

The company said it integrated deeply with major engines such as Unreal Engine, Unity and Godot, giving it the capability to support complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared wit the preview, Tencent said, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in the GameDev bench and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks, although the actual baseline numbers remain internal and weren’t released.

To advance scientific reasoning, Tencent advanced the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement to enhance research and development capabilities. Using the Hyra 2.0 harness, an autonomous AI research agent system, the model optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture.

The model is currently available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant, Ima and more. It can also be accessed via third-party sources such as OpenRouter, Hermes and OpenCode. The company added that, despite its significant enhancements over Hy4 Preview, it kept costs low, maintaining the same pricing at around 90 cents per million input tokens, $2.70 per million output tokens and 4.5 cents per million cached input tokens.

The Flash version of the model is scheduled for release soon to deliver greater cost efficiency for users. The company also said it intends to release the model weights and system cards in coming days.

#5559. Xavier Becerra Wins California’s Gubernatorial Election in a Landslide After Pledging To Tackle Housing Shortage

Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra has won the California gubernatorial contest, trouncing Donald Trump-endorsed Republican hopeful Steve Hilton in a landslide win.

The Associated Press called the race immediately after polls closed, reflecting Becerra's undeniable lead over his GOP opponent. The victory was part of Tuesday night's "blue wave," in which Democrats reclaimed control of both the House and the Senate.

"What a great night to be a Californian," Becerra said at a victory party in West Sacramento, CA. "What a great night to be an American."

In his concession speech, Hilton, 57, congratulated Becerra on his win, but also predicted that a Republican will become governor in 2030.

"Enjoy it while it lasts," he told his opponent.

Becerra, 68, who served as secretary of Health and Human Services under President Joe Biden, entered the midterm elections on Tuesday holding a commanding lead of 27 percentage points over Hilton, a Fox News contributor, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.

The decisive victory marks a historic milestone as Becerra becomes the first Latino elected as governor of California, and the first Latino to hold the office since Romualdo Pacheco, who was elevated to the post from lieutenant governor in 1875 following the resignation of Gov. Newton Booth.

Becerra will be sworn in on Jan. 4, 2027, replacing the term-limited Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who campaigned for his successor on Sunday alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris. Both Newsom and Harris are expected to consider presidential runs in 2028.

Becerra becomes California's third consecutive Democratic governor, cementing the party's dominance in the deep-blue state.

California's 41st governor inherits a tangle of economic challenges anchored by the state’s acute housing affordability crisis.

In the run-up to the election, Becerra, a former congressman, made housing one of the main pillars of his campaign, promising to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his very first day in office and appoint senior officials across state agencies who will be tasked with removing obstacles to construction projects.

Becerra’s ambitious platform includes proposals to enforce 90-day "shot clocks" for building permits to accelerate construction, slash impact fees, streamline reviews for modular homes, and overhaul financing for affordable housing.

"The Becerra win signals that California intends to keep pushing for more housing, with an approach aimed at making building simpler," says Realtor.com® economist Jiayi Xu. "Taken together, it points to California doubling down on a pro-supply approach."

For the nation's most populous state, these changes could not come soon enough: on this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California earned an F grade thanks to its to ultra-low housing affordability score.

Additionally, a Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and the Census Bureau's American Community Survey data found that the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to buy a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state behind Montana.

In a bid to unlock housing supply, Becerra plans to pursue zoning reforms, expand by-right approvals near job and transit hubs, and introduce more duplexes and small condos to put homeownership within reach of renters.

As part of his plan to tackle California’s entrenched homelessness epidemic through prevention, Becerra has proposed offering rental assistance to vulnerable families and bolstering tenant protections, which he views as more economical than spending thousands of dollars down the line on shelter beds.

Looking ahead, Xu expects Becerra to face significant hurdles, beginning with potential legal challenges and pushbacks on the housing front.

"For example, his plan targets lower impact fees, but some cities rely heavily on those fees to pay for infrastructure, and his campaign has not detailed how that lost revenue would be replaced," notes the economist. "A clearer plan for cities will be needed to win their cooperation."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5558. Louisiana Passes New Property Tax Relief Amendments for Seniors

On Tuesday, Louisiana voters passed four ballot measures on property tax exemptions, aimed at providing tax relief for seniors, surviving spouses of disabled veterans, and entrepreneurs who rehab dilapidated homes.

Voters passed Amendment 1 with 76% support. Amendment 1 allows the surviving spouse of a disabled veteran transfer the homestead property tax exemption to a new home.

Currently, disabled veterans receive a homestead property tax exemption that is commensurate with the degree of disability they experience. Spouses are able to maintain the exemption in the event of their veteran spouse passing away. However, this amendment allows a one-time opportunity to the surviving spouse to transfer the exemption to a new property as well.

The Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs as well as Leaders for a Better Louisiana and Louisiana Realtors® all expressed support for the measure.

Meanwhile, the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice opposed the measure, saying: "We support veterans and their families, but we do not need another special tax exception written into the state constitution."

Amendment 6 passed with 65% support. It proposes a property tax exemption of up to $30,000 for homeowners over age 65 who already qualify for an income assessment-based freeze.

Introduced by state Rep. Les Farnum, the amendment received support from both Democrats and Republicans.

The nonpartisan Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, and the nonprofit Pelican Institute for Public Policy all opposed the amendment.

In its explanation for its opposition to the amendment, Leaders for a Better Louisiana wrote: "While we like the idea of shielding senior citizens from taxes they have no control over...we wish it provided more flexibility for local governments to tailor tax breaks in a way that might be more suited to their individual goals and situations. As we have stated elsewhere, the better approach would be to untie the hands of local governments with regard to property taxes, rather than putting more rules in the constitution.The Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment: "No community is forced to do anything. Each one decides for itself whether helping its seniors age in place is worth it. That is how local control should work."

Meanwhile, 59% of voters supported Amendment 9, which raises the income level for seniors to qualify for a property tax freeze from $100,000 to $150,000, allowing more people to qualify for the freeze.

The amendment aims to offer increased financial relief to seniors, many of whom live on fixed incomes. Proponents argued that the amendment could attract more seniors to the state. Critics said it would further reduce the tax dollars local governments require for social services.

Currently, around 230,000 people qualify for the freeze in the state.

The last time voters approved an increase in the income limit for the special property tax assessment was in 2020, when voters approved an increase in income limit from $50,000 to $100,000.

Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment, saying that "the income limit to qualify has not kept pace with the cost of living."

Amendment 10, which allows communities to create optional property tax exemptions for blighted and derelict property that has been rehabilitated, also narrowly passed with 53% support.

Under the initiative, up to 75% of a rehabilitated property's assessed value would be exempt from property taxes for up to 20 years. Meanwhile, cleared lots would receive a 25% exemption on assessed value for up to 10 years as long as they weren't next to residential or commercial buildings.

Proponents argued this would incentivize the rehabilitation of derelict properties and positively impact the safety and well-being in a community. Communities could choose to opt in or out of the initiative depending on local needs.

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in Louisiana is 0.55%, which is relatively low compared with states like New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

#5557. Share of Adjustable Rate Mortgages Hits Highest Level Since September 2025

A house key sitting on mortgage application.To see more of my financial images click on the link below:

Mortgage rates ticked down a bit this past week but landing at 7.3%, it wasn’t enough to move the needle for buyers submitting loan applications for 30-year-fixed rate mortgages. Sitting almost a full percentage point lower, adjustable rate mortgages (ARMs) however continue to be attractive for buyers looking to start out with a lower monthly payment.

The latest Market Composite Index from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)—its measure of mortgage loan activity volume and includes purchases and refinances—shows mortgage application activity decreasing 1.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis after last week’s 3.4% increase. On an unadjusted basis, the Index decreased 2% compared with the previous week.

This week’s decline follows weeks of fluctuations as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate still lingers around 7.29%, according to Freddie Mac and this week currently sits at 7.25%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Freddie Mac’s next rate report will be released Thursday.

“Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting,” said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s SVP and chief economist. “While the 30-year rate declined to 7.3 percent, activity is still quite slow, with purchase application volume down for the week and refinance volume effectively flat at a very low level.”

MBA once again pointed to increased activity in the ARM share of total mortgage applications as a sign that buyers are ready to move on lower rates. According to the report, the average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.29% from 6.41%, with points decreasing to 1.00 from 1.20 (including the origination fee) for 80 percent LTV loans. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.4 percent of total applications, MBA reported.

“As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025,” Fratantoni said.

An ARM loan is where the interest rate is fixed for an initial period, typically five years, and then changes annually for the life of the loan, based on market conditions.

MBA’s Refinance Index increased 0.1% from the previous week and was 60% lower than the same week one year ago. MBA’s seasonally adjusted Purchase Index–its weekly measurement of nationwide home loan applications based on a sample of about 75% of U.S. mortgage activity–decreased 2% from one week earlier. The unadjusted Purchase Index decreased 4% compared with the previous week and was 19% lower than the same week one year ago, according to the report.

The refinance share of mortgage activity saw an increase this week–to 39.8% from 38.9% the previous week, MBA reported.

A look at government-backed loans this week shows the FHA share of total applications decreased to 16.0% from 16.6% the week prior. The VA share of total applications increased to 11.2% from 11.0% the week prior, and the USDA share of total applications increased to 0.6% from 0.5% the week prior.

#5556. VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

Broadcom Inc. is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities that simplify artificial intelligence workload deployment, strengthen infrastructure security and simplify disaster recovery.

The company is also introducing a lower-cost virtualization platform aimed at smaller customers that don’t need a full private cloud platform.

Today’s updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company’s flagship private cloud platform, and a collection of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom’s 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Prashanth Shenoy (pictured), Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability designed to simplify the initial configuration of private AI environments.

It combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow, replacing multiple manual configuration processes. “We have consolidated all of that, made a quick start workflow and streamlined the workflow completely so they can get it up and running day zero in a matter of minutes,” Shenoy said.

Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN. The feature, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release, supports AI applications that depend heavily on unstructured data and lets developers provision storage through self-service interfaces.

On the security front, Broadcom is incorporating additional capabilities directly into VCF rather than requiring customers to purchase them separately. These include confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, as well as planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom said the compliance features will continuously monitor infrastructure settings against industry benchmarks, identify configuration drift and provide remediation guidance.

The virtualization maker is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms. The capability will provide orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters.

Additional protection will be available through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication.

Two other advanced services, VMware Live Recovery and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management, address cyber recovery and continuous compliance enforcement for virtual machines and containers.

The company is also broadening its portfolio at the lower end with VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores. Based on vSphere 9, Express includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching.

Shenoy said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without purchasing the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms. “They don’t need a whole cloud in their two-server environment,” he said.

Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom didn’t disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.
