#5555. Gina Hinojosa Ousts Greg Abbott in Texas Governor’s Race—What Her Win Means for Housing

Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa made history Tuesday night, becoming the first Latina elected as governor of Texas and the first Democrat to win the office in 36 years.

Her victory was a major upset that denied Republican Greg Abbott a record-setting fourth term—and could signal a change in direction for the state's housing policies.

Hinojosa campaigned on making homeownership more attainable by restricting corporate investors, cutting residential property taxes, and cracking down on predatory rental practices.

The proposals put her on a different path from Abbott, who emphasized removing barriers to home construction and expanding the state's existing property tax relief. The Lone Star state is already the nation's largest homebuilder, accounting for 14.6% of all building permits issued, and received an A- on its Affordability Report Card from Realtor.com® in June.

Speaking to supporters in Austin, Hinojosa framed her victory as a rebuke of wealthy corporate interests and their influence over state government.

“Tonight, Texas, we answered—and we didn’t whisper," she said. "We answered loud enough for every billionaire, every lobbyist, and every corrupt politician in Austin to hear: Texas belongs to us."

One of Hinojosa's central housing promises is to curb corporate investors' purchases of single-family homes, which she argues have made it harder for ordinary Texans to compete for homeownership.

It's an issue she's been advocating for since her time in the state House. In 2025, Hinojosa introduced House Bill 2910, which would have prohibited covered corporate owners from holding more than 10 single-family rental properties in Texas.

Another proposal, House Bill 2334, would have prevented investment firms from entering contracts to purchase newly listed single-family homes during their first 30 days on the market.

Neither bill became law, but the state could be particularly fertile ground for the proposals.

"Texas is where this type of policy would bite hardest, though I'd still expect a modest effect on affordability," says Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com.

Megainvestors accounted for 1.9% of all home purchases in Texas during the first half of 2026, the highest share of any state and roughly three times the national rate of 0.6%, according to Jones' research.

And in some markets, corporate buyers are even more concentrated. Investors accounted for 15.9% of home purchases in San Antonio, 15.6% in Dallas-Fort Worth, 13.5% in Houston, and 12.4% in Austin, according to research from Realtor.com.

In three of those four markets, investors purchased homes at prices substantially below the overall median, suggesting that competition remains concentrated in the more affordable segments of the housing market.

A federal law enacted in July will prohibit institutional investors controlling 350 or more single-family homes from purchasing additional properties beginning in January 2027, subject to certain exceptions—but "Hinojosa’s cap goes further than the federal law," according to Jones.

Still, she cautions that limiting corporate purchases would address only a fraction of the forces keeping homeownership out of reach.

"The effect on homeownership is limited because the policy only touches that segment, which is a small slice of total purchases," she explains, noting that housing supply, mortgage rates, insurance, and property taxes remain bigger drivers of affordability.

"Build-to-rent is the key question," Jones says, referring to developments constructed specifically as rental housing. The federal law exempts qualifying build-to-rent projects, but Hinojosa's proposal did not explicitly offer the same protection.

"Limiting investor [single-family rental] supply would more likely push rents up than down, which works against the affordability goal."

Hinojosa has also promised to address rental practices, including landlords' use of algorithmic pricing software and rent increases imposed during the application process.

Texas has been one of the nation's most welcoming markets for data centers, attracting tech giants with cheap land, abundant energy and generous tax incentives. The state accounts for an estimated quarter of U.S. data center capacity planned by 2030, according to Reuters.

But growing opposition over electricity costs, water consumption, and other neighborhood impacts has begun changing that equation. About 61% of National Association of Realtor members said their clients were concerned that data centers would raise energy costs, and 56% reported concerns about water usage, according to survey data released in September.

It was enough to make Abbott—once an enthusiastic supporter of the industry—halt new data center permits in September, pending an environmental and energy audit.

Now, Hinojosa has promised to go further, calling for a legislatively backed moratorium, greater local control over development, and protections against data center-driven utility increases.

Her victory heightened concerns that Texas could become a more difficult place to build. Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX fell Wednesday as investors weighed the prospect of tighter restrictions.

Hinojosa and Abbott both campaigned on cutting homeowners' property taxes, but differed over how to pay for that relief.

In 2025, Texas raised its school district homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000, saving homeowners hundreds of dollars annually—a measure that Hinojosa voted in favor of.

Now, she wants to go further by eliminating corporate subsidies and using the savings to reduce residential property taxes, with the eventual goal of eliminating them altogether.

Abbott, meanwhile, proposed eliminating school district property taxes on owner-occupied homes, using state surpluses to replace the lost revenue.

The proposals also reflect differences over public education. Abbott championed a $1 billion private-school voucher program in 2025, while also signing an $8.5 billion public school funding package. Hinojosa opposed the vouchers and has pledged to repeal the program while increasing support for public schools and teachers.

But her tax plan faces a substantial funding question: Replacing homeowners' school maintenance-and-operations property taxes alone would cost an estimated $8.6 billion annually. Hinojosa has yet to detail how eliminating corporate subsidies would cover that cost without reducing school funding.

Hinojosa will take office in January 2027, but many of her proposed housing reforms would require the approval of state lawmakers.

And while Tuesday's elections changed the political landscape in Austin, it didn't guarantee Hinojosa a friendly Legislature. Democrat Vikki Goodwin unseated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, giving Democrats leadership of the state Senate. Republicans, however, are expected to retain their majority in that chamber.

Meanwhile, control of the Texas House remained undecided Wednesday morning. Democrats needed to flip 14 seats to take control for the first time since 2003, and were gaining ground in several Republican-held districts.

But even if Democrats capture the House, Hinojosa would still need Republican support in the Senate to advance her housing agenda.

The newly elected governor seemed undaunted Tuesday night, closing her victory speech by invoking her grandmother's advice: "No te dejes," she said, which loosely translates to "don't let yourself get pushed around."

Hinojosa's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

#5554. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

#5553. A 1970s Hollywood Hills Home Was Reimagined With a ‘Floating’ Canyon Pool and Midcentury Soul

A sleek Nichols Canyon estate in Los Angeles, perched above the treetops, has recently hit the market for $4,994,000.

Built in 1978, the four-bedroom home has been entirely reimagined by an acclaimed design studio and now offers a timeless 2,798-square-foot floor plan.

“Ome Dezin acquired the property in 2025 with a clear vision to reimagine and resell it, completing the renovation in October 2026,” says listing agent Claire O’Connor of Compass. “What made this home compelling was its inherent architectural character.

"Rather than strip away its identity, they saw an opportunity to build upon it, creating something that feels distinctly contemporary while remaining rooted in its 1970s origins.”

Set on nearly half an acre, the hillside retreat has wood ceilings, exposed beams, marble, wood, and terrazzo floors, built-ins, and three fireplaces.

“Entertaining feels intrinsic to the architecture rather than an afterthought,” O’Connor said. “The interiors unfold naturally toward the outdoor spaces, culminating in a dramatic infinity pool suspended above the canyon. There’s an intimacy to the scale that makes it equally suited to a quiet evening or a gathering of friends. It’s a home that encourages connection without feeling performative.”

An expansive deck overlooks the infinity-edge pool, which is cantilevered over the hillside to create the illusion of floating above the canyon.

“I see this appealing to a buyer who values provenance and individuality over square footage,” she noted. “There’s a growing sophistication among luxury buyers in Los Angeles, with an increasing appreciation for homes that feel curated rather than manufactured. This is someone who recognizes that true luxury isn’t necessarily about having more, but about finding something that can’t easily be replicated.”

O’Connor notes that the home’s location in Nichols Canyon is “a particularly interesting position in Los Angeles."

"It offers an almost pastoral sense of seclusion within minutes of Hollywood and the Sunset Strip," she says.

"The winding roads, mature landscape, and dramatic topography create a sense of discovery that’s increasingly rare in the city. It’s that tension between urban proximity and natural isolation that makes it so desirable."

#5552. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5551. Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results

Smartsheet Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence-powered planning and execution platform designed to help enterprises identify when projects are veering off course and take corrective action before delays and cost overruns become serious problems.

Announced at the company’s Engage 2026 conference, the new vsActual platform — pronounced “versus actual” — uses AI agents to continuously monitor work across multiple enterprise systems, compare progress against strategic objectives and recommend adjustments. The company also announced new agentic workflow capabilities, integrations and security controls for its existing work management platform.

The centerpiece of vsActual is what Smartsheet calls Execution Graph, a knowledge graph built from what the company said are two decades of workflow data encompassing millions of projects and nine petabytes of information. The graph maps relationships between tasks, projects, programs and strategic objectives to help AI agents understand how changes in one part of an organization affect others.

The company’s goal is to address a growing disconnect between individual productivity improvements enabled by AI and measurable organizational results, said Pratima Arora, Smartsheet’s chief product and technology officer.

“We were seeing a lot of intelligence and productivity gains getting stuck at an individual level and not translating to a team and organization level,” she said.

VsActual is designed to operate across existing enterprise applications rather than require organizations to consolidate work onto a single platform. It can connect to applications from Oracle Corp., SAP SE, Workday Inc., Atlassian Corp. PLC and ServiceNow Inc. to gather information about budgets, schedules, staffing and project dependencies.

Smartsheet said AI agents can turn strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget proposals into structured plans, model alternative scenarios and monitor execution against those plans. A drift-detection agent (pictured) continuously searches for emerging problems, while other agents generate executive reports and recommend changes as business priorities evolve.

The system can also trace the consequences of disruptions across organizational hierarchies. “If there is a delay in a Jira ticket that has impact five levels up, we can detect it and tell you what is happening,” Arora said.

Smartsheet said its historical workflow data provides an advantage over competing planning and work management products. Execution Graph builds on an existing Amazon Web Services Inc. Neptune knowledge graph containing approximately 100 million nodes and incorporates information about workflow patterns, dependencies and collaboration, Arora said.

The company uses multiple foundation models, selecting them based on workload requirements and cost. AWS and Databricks Inc. are its major underlying technology providers. Arora said Smartsheet isn’t training its own large language models.

The announcements also expand Smartsheet’s existing AI capabilities. New Agentic Workflows allow users to schedule recurring activities such as status reports and risk assessments. Specialized creation and data-quality agents can generate project structures, dashboards and reports or identify problems in underlying data.

New integrations include native connections to ServiceNow, Microsoft Corp. Dynamics 365, HubSpot Inc. customer relationship management, Workday Inc. human resources software and Intuit Inc.’s QuickBooks. Conversational integrations with GitHub, Zendesk Inc., Airtable and Monday.com Ltd. are entering early access, with additional AI-assisted integrations planned for early 2027.

Arora emphasized that agentic workflows combine conventional automation with AI rather than relying exclusively on large language models. “This industry overuses LLMs sometimes where it is just simple deterministic action,” she said.

Although some agents can execute scheduled tasks automatically, Arora said human approval remains the default approach for consequential actions. “Our default stance is human in the loop,” she said.

The compay also announced International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 42001 certification, security event streaming and data classification capabilities intended to strengthen oversight of AI operations.

Smartsheet developed vsActual with about a dozen enterprise design partners. The company publishes pricing on its website.

#5550. DC Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George Promises 72,000 New Housing Units

Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected the first new mayor of Washington, DC, in 12 years after breezing past a crowded field to cap off a campaign focused on affordability.

The Associated Press called the election for Lewis George before 7 p.m. Tuesday, reflecting her commanding lead over Rhonda Hamilton, a community advocate running as an independent; Robert L. Gross, representing the DC Statehood Green Party, and 11 write-in candidates. That race did not include a Republican contender.

The win potentially places Lewis George, a 38-year-old D.C. Council member, on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who previously labeled her a "communist" and suggested that she was a threat to the safety and prosperity of the nation's capital.

"The people of D.C. elect the mayor of D.C., and I am willing to work with this administration to the benefit of D.C. residents," Lewis George told FOX 5 DC after her victory. "And I'm also willing to stand up to this administration when it comes to doing just that."

Lewis George will replace outgoing Democratic Mayor Muriel Bowser, who decided last year not to seek reelection for a fourth term.

"Congratulations to Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George," Bowser wrote on X Wednesday morning. "I’ll run through the tape and support a seamless transition. I love you, DC."

When she is sworn in on Jan. 2, Lewis George will become DC's first democratic socialist mayor, joining the ranks of New York City's Zohran Mamdani, Seattle's Katie Wilson, and Mayor-elect David Morales, of Providence, RI.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is her "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout DC within five years.

Additional housing-related planks in the mayor-elect's platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest American Community Survey numbers from the U.S. Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in DC have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

On the broader affordability front, Lewis-George campaigned on lowering utility bills for the district's 700,000 residents and pushing through universal affordable child care.

Lewis George easily won the Democratic primary in June, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said after her victory that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and threatened to carry out a federal takeover of DC if she won.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Lewis George responded at the time that threatening the revocation of the city's home rule "because you do not like how residents vote is an attack on democracy itself."

However, now that the Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate, DC is expected to be shielded from Trump's potential efforts to encourch on its autonomy, since it is the Congress, not the president, that has legislative power over the district, according to the Associated Press.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5548. Inside Joe Rogan’s Incredible $14.4 Million Austin Mansion—and Home to His Very Controversial Podcast

Podcaster Joe Rogan has once again found himself at the center of controversy after he was confronted about his past political views.

Rogan, 59, was on the receiving end of scrutiny when comedian Sam Tallent called Rogan out for voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

"Dude it's weird, cuz like, I talk to people a lot who I don't share like, the exact ideals with, like, I don't like that you f—n' endorsed Trump, but like, I have a lot of friends who voted for Trump," Tallent said.

Tallent added, "No, it's fine. Listen, it used to be that people used to be able to differ in their opinions and have conversations. But today we have become so divided, and I think a big factor is social media, echo chambers, propaganda, bots, gaslighting. And it seems like there's so much riding on everything constantly, because you're looking at your phone all the time.

"And everything on the phone is, 'This is the end. This is the end, this is the beginning of the end, this is a signal of the end, the only hope is to stop this,' and on both sides. People are addicted to their phones, so like, the information you're getting almost all day long is very bleak and very dire."

Rogan's podcast has long been known as a hotspot for the internet personality to share his outspoken opinions on everything from from celebrity gossip to political policy.

"The Joe Rogan Experience," which he records largely at his $14.4 million home in Austin, TX, is widely regarded as one of the most successful podcasts in the world, but it seems listeners on Apple have a different opinion.

Rogan, who drew a gargantuan audience with his three-hour-long interview with Trump during his campaign for president, has seen his podcast tumble down the Apple rankings of most popular shows—falling to third place, behind the New York Times' "The Daily" and a true-crime hit called "Crime Junkie."

The news came shortly before Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko accused the podcaster of "pushing Russian propaganda on his podcast," amid the war in Ukraine. Klitschko slammed Rogan's comments about President Joe Biden's decision to provide U.S.-made missiles to Ukrainian forces.

In a previous episode with music producer Scott Storch, the two discussed their relief that Trump had won the election, and then criticized the Biden administration for providing Ukraine with long-range missiles for use in its war with Russia.

“I feel safer knowing that Trump is in office,” Storch told Rogan.

“What I don’t feel safer about is that now they’re launching missiles into Russia,” Rogan replied. “How are you allowed to do that when you’re on the way out? [There] should be, like, some sort of, like, a pause for, like, significant actions that could potentially start World War III.

“Yeah, [Vladimir] Putin should not have invaded Ukraine, yes, 100%, but don’t start World War III,” Rogan added.

In a video response, Klitschko addressed Rogan directly: “You talk about these American weapons being sent to Ukraine, which you believe will lead to the third World War.

“So, let me tell you that you’re repeating Russian propaganda. Putin’s Russia is in trouble, so they want to scare you and people like you.”

He added, “Putin’s Russia wants to destroy Ukraine quietly, they want America to stay quiet. Not great, but quiet. A great America is not an America that abandons countries that defend freedom with their lives.”

Klitschko offered to come on Rogan's podcast so they could further discuss the topic as "free men."

Rogan is no stranger to provoking outrage and controversy with his comments, and his show retains the top spot in Spotify's rankings. However, his lackluster showing in the Apple charts will no doubt come as something of a surprise to the podcaster.

Indeed, Rogan's show has proven so popular that even Vice President Kamala Harris reportedly considered an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." She ultimately opted for the more female-focused "Call Her Daddy" with host Alexandra Cooper.

Still, the podcaster has managed to lure dozens of A-list celebrities to his new $14.4 million home on Lake Austin in Texas, where he moved to from California in 2020, and where he has built a custom studio to record his show.

Rogan, a former comedian, previously provided UFC color commentary before launching his podcast in 2009. By 2015, he was one of the most popular podcasters.

Rogan interviewed everyone from Edward Snowden to Neil deGrasse Tyson, J.D. Vance, and Bernie Sanders. (After Sanders appeared on his show in 2020, Rogan endorsed the Democratic Party candidate in the 2020 presidential race.)

In 2020, Rogan moved from Southern California to Austin after reportedly agreeing to an estimated $100 million deal to broadcast exclusively with Spotify.

In February 2024, Rogan reportedly signed a new $250 million agreement with Spotify that allowed him to broadcast on other platforms, including YouTube and Apple.

That same year, Rogan opened up about his decision to relocate to Texas, explaining that California's strict COVID-19 restrictions were partly to blame.

"Everything’s shut down, everything’s staying shut down," he recalled of the pandemic in California. "All my friends that were in the restaurant industry were struggling.

"I started looking out here in May [of that year], and I went to a restaurant with my kids, and they were like, 'We don’t have to wear a mask? We could eat at a restaurant?' Then we went to the lake, and people are playing music and jumping in the water, and [my children] were like, 'We want to live here!

"That was it. Two months later I lived here."

In 2022, he explained that he believed he would find "more freedom" in Texas than he was able to enjoy on the West Coast.

Since his Texas move, he seems to be recording shows in a studio built inside his sleek mansion, which sits right on Lake Austin.

Rogan's 4-acre property comes with 300 feet of Lake Austin frontage, according to the original listing. The 11,000-square-foot mansion was built in 2008 and offers eight bedrooms and 10 baths.

The parklike surroundings include “views of the lake and the undeveloped preserve land on the opposite side.” There are three docks, a pool, and terraces.

The mansion features a formal dining room with built-ins, a dual-island kitchen with a casual eating area, a living area with floor-to-ceiling windows, and an office. A gym can also be found on the grounds.

Rogan's Instagram account reveals several upgrades he made in addition to his studio, including a cold plunge tub and a sauna.

The locale, not far from downtown Austin but seemingly a world away, was a draw for Hollywood A-lister Sandra Bullock, who reportedly owns a home in the area.

Originally from the East Coast, she now lives in San Francisco.

#5547. University AI’s biggest challenge? Scaling research without losing control

The push for sovereign AI is reaching university research labs, where control over data, models and compute now shapes what science gets done.

Universities sit at an unusual crossroads in the current technological shift, as their work spans open education and tightly controlled federal research. Learning sits at the heart of both missions, making AI a core supporting technology for expanding research and education alike, according to Vince Kellen (pictured, center), chief information officer of the Texas A&M University System.

“AI is a platform for thought. It’s a platform for discovery,” Kellen noted. “AI kind of undergirds all of what we’re going to be doing in the future — certainly what we’re doing in the present now.”

Kellen and Casey Bryan (right), chief information officer of the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station, spoke with Krista Case (left) during theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. They discussed how Texas A&M is building a secure, controlled foundation for AI-driven research. (* Disclosure below.)

The foundation of Texas A&M’s approach is IGNITE, short for Innovative Growth in Next Generation AI Technology Ecosystem. It is a state-funded AI and high-performance computing platform led by TEES, as the experiment station is known. Dell Technologies Inc. is building the system with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. graphics processing units inside an Equinix Inc. data center in Dallas. That investment will give research teams the computing power their existing systems lack, Bryan noted.

“Part of our current challenge is that existing resources, while they are performing some of that work, are severely underpowered,” he said. “Research is getting done but could be helped by capacity and scale, which I think IGNITE’s going to bring to the table.”

But the economics matter as much as the capability. Public attention has centered on neoclouds and cloud providers, yet on-premises data centers are growing significantly because of both security controls and cost, according to Kellen. High retail prices for AI computing resources are now limiting the ability of institutions to conduct scientific research.

“There’s no way we could take the science to your classic neocloud provider today and conduct the same thing,” Kellen said. “It’s 5 to 10x the cost.”

Controlling those assets significantly reduces costs and strengthens security, Kellen said. Sovereignty spans four pillars — data, infrastructure, capability and model, and governance — with Equinix supplying physical protection for the compute itself, Bryan added. As a state agency, TEES follows National Institute of Standards and Technology frameworks 800-53 and 800-171, as well as Texas Administrative Code 202, and it wants IGNITE to be ready for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2.

“There’s a lot of controls we have to inherit, but our researchers shouldn’t have to think about all those,” Bryan said. “It should be absolutely seamless when they go to use the capabilities.”

That principle shaped the IGNITE build. When TEES sat down with Dell’s implementation team to schedule workshops, security came first, and the project’s architecture review board has since affirmed that direction, according to Bryan. For institutions starting their own sovereign AI projects, that sequencing is the lesson.

“The idea was to build that security foundation with which all of the other operational components could be built and referenced back to,” Bryan said. “At its core, start with security early — get it embedded in the process earlier on — and it’s much easier to keep it baked in at the beginning than have to worry about adding that at the end.”

#5543. Milwaukee Brewers Captain Christian Yelich Lists Newly Built Malibu Mansion for $30 Million

Milwaukee Brewers captain Christian Yelich is looking to shed his contemporary Malibu mansion, listing the hillside estate for $30 million.

The World Series champion purchased the 1-acre property for $5.55 million in 2020. At the time, the lot included “fully approved plans” from architect Michael Kovac of KOVAC Design Studio.

The 5,300-square-foot residence was completed this year, according to Architectural Digest. A KOVAC representative told the publication that Yelich plans to move his family to Wisconsin.

The 34-year-old baseball star has been romantically linked to professional soccer player, Paige Noel Almendariz, although it is not clear if the couple live together.

“Set in the heart of Malibu, this one-of-a-kind coastal retreat has been thoughtfully rebuilt from the ground up with an unwavering commitment to quality, design, and comfort,”reads the listing, which is held by Yelich’s mother, Alecia Yelich with Compass.

Her bio notes that professional athlete relocation is her speciality.

“Offering sweeping views of the Queen’s Necklace, Surfrider Beach, Pacific Coast Highway and Nobu, this is the kind of property that rarely comes to market,” the listing continues. “Every inch of the home has been carefully curated, blending sophisticated finishes with cutting-edge technology to create a living experience that is both luxurious and effortless.”

The home boasts four bedrooms, four full bathrooms, a powder room, a dedicated pool bathroom, and an outdoor shower.

Nestled in a light-flooded corner of the home with retractable glass walls that let in fresh air, the primary suite is truly astonishing. Even the soaking tub and walk-in shower have killer views.

The five additional bathrooms are impressive, as well, offering expansive windows and closets equipped with refrigerators in each room.

Custom hardwood floors imported from France run throughout the home for a touch of warmth, both aesthetically and through the radiant-heated flooring that complements them.

Floor-to-ceiling windows can also be found across the home, making the idyllic Malibu surroundings feel like part of the decor.

The chef’s kitchen offers sprawling counter space, chic modern fixtures, and plenty of storage for snacks, supplies, and cooking gadgets.

The kitchen sink faces the home’s breathtaking ocean views, while automated pocket doors seamlessly connect the room to the picturesque outdoor living space.

The home has a number of standout spaces to use for entertaining guests or to enjoy on a quiet night in, including the custom wet bar and a private cinema with a dedicated concession room, an LED video wall, luxury seating, immersive surround sound, and professional acoustic treatments.

Technology has been carefully incorporated into the dwelling, which the listing describes as a “fully integrated smart home,” which gives residents the opportunity to “effortless control lighting, climate, entertainment, shades, security, and access from a single platform.”

A custom two-car carage and newly-constructed sealed driveway provide a safe space for residents’ vehicles.

Outdoor living was considered as thoughtfully as the interiors, with the backyard anchored by a resort-style infinity-edge pool.

There’s no shortage of lounge space, with multiple entertaining spaces spread among the area’s various decks and patios, and fire features and outdoors amenities to be enjoyed. An outdoor kitchen and barbecue area are also perfectly-suited for hosting.

Fully-automated Tuuci umbrellas leverage integrated heaters to provide shade from the sun or warmth during a chilly night.

There is even an oversized fully-enclosed outdoor television; a state-of-the-art addition that’s designed to provide “a remarkable viewing experience even in the brightest Malibu sunshine.”

Prospective buyers with pets will also be thrilled to learn there’s also a custom dog run.

#5542. Oracle urges database customers to prepare for quantum security risks

Attackers can copy encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers mature, making quantum-resistant cryptography a present-day concern.

Oracle Corp. is applying the philosophy behind its security controls beneath AI agents to encryption across database fleets, according to Vipin Samar (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, database security, at Oracle.

“Even though we don’t have quantum computers which are sufficiently powerful today, when they come, that can create a risk because people can make a copy of your encrypted data today,” Samar said. “Your TLS 1.2 traffic, 1.3 traffic, I can make a copy of it. And then when quantum becomes available, I can figure out the session key and decrypt … your entire sensitive data.”

Samar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed security concerns related to quantum-resistant cryptography. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s new Cryptographic Posture Assessment in Oracle Data Safe assesses cryptographic configurations across database fleets, flagging weak spots such as lingering TLS 1.0 and 1.1 support. Agentic AI-driven remediation is in preview, Samar noted.

“It doesn’t help if network encryption is strong, but other parts are actually on the weaker side. And this becomes a challenge, especially when PQC or the quantum computers come along because they can attempt to hack into any of those systems,” Samar said.

Deep Data Security, which enforces row- and column-level access in Oracle AI Database 26ai, uses signed OAuth2 tokens to identify the end user behind an AI agent’s query. Oracle treats AI as one more application accessing the same data.

“We said instead of sprinkling this dust everywhere, why don’t we secure at the source?” Samar said. “When you move something inside the database, you get great security because there are no ways to bypass it.”

#5541. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. Know a home with a story worth telling? Nominate it for inclusion in the creative franchise using this form. Tour the first properties and get an alert when each new home debuts using redfin.com/iconic-homes.

#5540. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5539. United Wholesale Mortgage Pushes Through Q3 Amid Headwinds, Predicts Steady Q4

Despite having lower margins for the third quarter, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) Chairman, President and CEO Mat Ishbia stated that he feels prepared to handle “headwinds in the industry” during the company’s third quarter earnings call.

On the call, Ishbia referenced the challenges the mortgage market has faced within the past five years, saying that the market is “showing a lot of warts on a lot of different companies.”

“Everyone’s got some issue,” he stated. “A lot of other people are operating holes where they don’t have enough business. They don’t have enough opportunity to get loans, they can’t keep up production and they can’t invest in AI.”

Interest rates have weighed on the housing market heavily as of late, leaving mortgage lenders with lower demand. For UWM’s earnings however, Ishbia attributes the company’s success to the recent Oaktree partnership, which came together after an ugly bidding war with CrossCountry Mortgage.

“The best way to hedge is to do a lot more loans when rates drop, as long as you can stomach the Mortgage Servicing Right (MSR) values going down because rates drop,” Ishbia added. “We have a great hedging policy and process. We partnered with Oaktree on that and Vandy Fartaj. We feel really good about the process of how we’re hedging and how much to hedge, versus how much not to hedge.”

The latest Federal Reserve meeting in October concluded with no changes to rates, but mortgage rates have slowly begun to inch downward to the lower 7% range—around 7.24% according to Freddie Mac—after spiking dramatically from the September meeting’s rate hike.

“I think the natural hedge is the best way to do it, and we’re not back to the natural hedge yet,” he said.

Although the quarter’s loan origination volume came in at $33.4 billion—down from Q2 which was $39.7 billion, and the first quarter at $44.9 billion—Ishbia mentioned that expenses were down substantially, specifically tied into investments with AI technology.

“Those (expenses) are really just tied to the investments we’ve made in AI and technology over the last couple years when everyone thought our expenses were higher,” he noted. “And so we’re starting to see the fruits of our labor.”

In total, Q3 revenue clocked in around $811.1 million, which is down from last quarter’s $888 million and slightly down from last year’s revenue of around $843 million.

Adjusted EBITDA came in at $178.3 million, less than last quarter and last year’s estimates ($185.9 million and $211.1 million, respectively).

UWM’s stock grew following the earnings call, as the earnings report beat out expectations. The company’s stock jumped nearly 13%, but is still down about 59% year to date.

Net loss was down quarterly in Q3, to $212.6 million compared to Q2 at $451.9 million. It was significantly higher than last year’s Q3 net loss however ($12.1 million). As an improvement from the previous quarter, Ishbia again credits the lower expenses to the company’s AI investments now panning out.

“AI can definitely help you cut costs and expenses, and you’re seeing some of that benefit, but you have to make a massive investment in it to do that. As you can see, it helps you do more loans, grow your business and drive the top line revenue,” he commented.

As for market share, Ishbia emphasizes the power and role brokers play in UWM’s success. He described brokers as the “growing channel” and states that they are the “winners right now.”

“UWM’s market share is fantastic. We’re strong, we’re dominant, and we’re going to continue to grow. If we lose market share, I hope that happens because that means the broker market has gotten so big and it’s going to keep growing, that’s my focus,” he continued. “My focus is growing the broker channel, helping every loan officer do a little bit more loans, helping every real estate agent that works with brokers do more business, and helping them all win.”

With 2026 winding down, Ishbia sees the upcoming year as a time of “optimization” but said he expected the mortgage market to remain tough for some time. He also notes that UWM focuses primarily on purchase mortgages, and acknowledges the challenges that refinance mortgage loans could face with current rates.

“Since we’re mostly purchase, I’m not as concerned about the volume going down as much as a lot of refinance shops will,” he concluded. “Traditionally, the fourth quarter and first quarter are always the tougher times in the mortgage market. But once again, expenses are down, AI is winning and brokers are growing. We feel like we’re in the best position of anybody to capitalize on opportunity.”

#5538. Katy Perry’s Proposed Youth Summer Camp Sparks Wildfire Concern From Santa Barbara Residents

Katy Perry’s Firework Foundation has proposed a youth summer camp just outside of her hometown of Santa Barbara, CA, but nearly 400 residents are opposing the plan, citing a laundry list of concerns from wildfire risk to traffic and noise.

According to the project’s website, Gratitude Canyon “would provide a permanent home for Camp Firework” at a Goleta property that formerly operated as the headquarters of Bragg Live Food Products—the company that popularized apple cider vinegar.

Gratitude Canyon explains that the pop star and her sister, Angela Lerche—the foundation’s president—spent “significant time” at the proposed site of the camp growing up, noting a “close friendship” with Patricia Bragg, the company’s former CEO who died in 2023 at the age of 94.

The foundation estimates that “approximately 97% of the roughly 110-acre property would remain open space, agriculture or landscaping,” and that the camp’s activity would be “concentrated on about 16 acres,” leaving “much” of the existing apple orchard to remain.

The County of Santa Barbara's Major Condition Use Permit Application Project Description supports those claims.

The program has operated for seven years across more than a dozen camp sites, and serves children ages 11 through 13, combining “art, nature, leadership, and relationship-building for young people who may not otherwise have access to immersive camp experiences.”

A petition under the name “Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon” has garnered 396 signatures from concerned residents in response to the way the project is “currently proposed.”

“The Firework Foundation is seeking County approval to rezone 183 Winchester Canyon with a General Plan Amendment and build a youth camp/event center, bringing 8,000+ visitors a year into a quiet, residential canyon, with amplified noise permitted 9am-9pm, 400-person events, and one way in or out of a high fire-risk, debris-flow zone,” the petition states.

Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon has organized the neighbors’ “top concerns.” The first on the list is that they believe the camp is a “Trojan Horse” and is a “year-round event center” designed “under the guise of a summer camp for underserved kids.”

However, Gratitude Canyon has stated that the proposal is not intended to serve as “a wedding or concert venue,” and plans to keep limited use outside of summer camp to schools, nonprofits, and “occasional retreats,” as well as “no more than four special events per year.”

Additionally, the petition raises concerns about fire safety, claiming “a formal fire protection plan and independent county-reviewed evacuation analysis still haven’t been completed,” and that evacuation capacity for the camp’s children and staff should be established prior to changing the property’s zoning.

However, Gratitude Canyon’s frequently asked questions page notes “fire prevention has been incorporated into the project form the earliest planning stages” and claim “measures include defensible space, vegetation management, emergency access, onsite water, hardened structures, evacuation planning, emergency communications, and 24-hour staffing while campers are onsite.”

The Gratitude Canyon website also explains that the Firework Foundation is engaging “directly with neighbors” and that the project “remains an evolving proposal.”

The summer camp proposal is not the first time Perry has been involved in a dispute centered around property in Santa Barbara.

The “California Gurls” singer and her former fiance, Orlando Bloom, were involved in a yearslong courtroom battle regarding a $15 million Montecito mansion.

The legal drama began in 2020, when the couple purchased the home from 1-800-Flowers founder, Carl Westcott, who rescinded the deal days later.

Westcott had reportedly purchased the estate for $11 million just two months prior, and sued Perry’s long-time business manager, Bernie Gudvi, who handled the purchase. Westcott claimed he “lacked capacity” to sell his home because he was suffering from a brain disorder and was under the influence of painkillers.

After years of legal back-and-forth, a 2023 ruling concluded that the original sale contract should be upheld. Perry countersued Westcott, seeking nearly $6 million in damages from the veteran, including $3.5 million in lost rental income and more than $2 million in repairs due to his alleged “lack of maintenance” of the property. The damages were later revised to $4.8 million.

Perry was awarded $1.94 million in damages, which was deducted from the $6 million that remained outstanding on the property’s original purchase price, leaving Perry and her representatives responsible for paying just over $4 million.

In October of this year, Westcott alleged he had only received a fraction of the amount owed, leaving Perry and Bloom susceptible to another legal confrontation.

#5537. Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push. The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer is not a human necessarily,” Agarwal said. “The need for real-time access is a lot more with AI.”

#5536. Beyond the Zero Down Payment: The Best States for Homebuyers Using VA Loans in 2026

VA loans can help veterans and active-duty service members turn their dream of homeownership into a reality.

Partly guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, they don’t require down payments or charge monthly mortgage insurance, unlike many other loan programs.

If you or a loved one are eligible for a VA loan, you may be wondering where to buy a home. According to Military.com, Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee are all solid options.

“What makes these states attractive isn't necessarily one standout benefit. It's the combination of things that can make life after the military a little easier, whether that's keeping more of your retirement income, finding a good civilian job, or living somewhere with a strong veteran community,” says Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United Home Loans in Columbia, MO.

By becoming familiar with what each state has to offer, you could narrow down your home search and find a property that aligns with your lifestyle budget.

From no property taxes and lower housing costs to veteran-specific tax breaks, these military-friendly states can make homeownership more accessible and affordable.

According to data from the VA, Virginia is one of the leading states for VA-backed loans, likely due to its large military population and steady real estate market growth.

“Northern Virginia’s proximity to government facilities like the Pentagon, Fort Belvoir, and Marine Corps Base Quantico allows many veterans to transition into federal or defense-related employment without uprooting their families,” says Dell Jeanty, real estate agent at Dell Residential in Arlington, VA.

The state offers real estate tax exemption for qualifying veterans with a 100% service-connected, permanent and total disability. Additionally, due to the major military installations and frequent military relocations, Virginia has a high concentration of assumable loans.

“This means you could potentially take over a seller's lower, locked-in historical interest rate and further your savings as a veteran,” Jeanty adds.

Many markets in North Carolina, including Charlotte, offer opportunities for veterans at different stages of life, whether you’re transitioning to a civilian career or retiring.

“There’s an established veteran community and plenty of ways to build new connections through work, recreation, and shared interests. You can choose city living or quieter settings with more land while enjoying professional sports, outdoor activities, and travel access,” says Ashley Horton, global real estate adviser at Premier Sotheby's International Realty in Charlotte.

Also, military installations across the Carolinas like Fort Liberty and Camp Lejeune are within driving distance, and highway connections and a major airport keep you connected to other markets. Plus, North Carolina lets qualifying military retirees deduct military retirement pay from state taxable income.

“Compared with markets in other states, those in North Carolina can give you more home, more space, and more options for the same budget. If you’re relocating from higher-cost cities, the equity from your previous home can stretch further here,” adds Horton.

Florida is one of those states where you’ll never run out of things to do.

You can enjoy country living with land and wide-open spaces, a coastal environment with beautiful beaches and waterways, or a neighborhood close to shopping, restaurants, and entertainment. And of course, you can’t beat being able to enjoy the outdoors almost year-round.

“I live and sell in the Orlando area, which is most well known for the Disney and Universal theme parks. In fact, Universal Studios Orlando just opened the Epic Universe park—fun for the whole family,” says Christina Rordam, a real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando.

Also, since there are fewer homebuyers to compete with in Florida, you may have more leverage to negotiate ideal terms.

According to Rordam, there are currently two groups of sellers: the motivated and the unrealistic.

“The motivated home sellers are moving for job transfers, divorcing, having kids, and needing more space. These types of life events really encourage sellers to take a long, hard look at the current market and cut buyers a good deal,” Rordam explains.

In the past, it was almost unthinkable to negotiate price, repairs, and closing costs. Now, it's much more likely.

Rordam has a cash buyer for whom she negotiated $1,600 in repairs and $20,000 off the purchase price on a home that had been on the market less than a week.

In addition, Florida has no state individual income tax and some valuable property tax benefits for qualifying veterans.

“For example, certain veterans with service-connected disabilities may qualify for additional homestead property tax exemptions, and veterans with qualifying total and permanent service–connected disabilities may be eligible for a full exemption from property taxes on their homestead. Those savings can make a real difference in the overall cost of owning a home,” says Sheena Haney, broker and owner at Haney Signature Realty in St. Augustine, FL.

To Haney, Florida is more than just a place to buy a home.

“It’s a place where you can really enjoy the lifestyle, raise a family, retire, and make lasting memories,” adds Haney.

Texas gives veteran buyers something incredibly valuable: options.

In Central Texas, for example, you’ll find everything from established neighborhoods to new construction, where builders may offer incentives to make homeownership more affordable.

“San Antonio is especially attractive because of its relatively low cost of living, allowing many military families to stretch their housing budgets further,” says April Guerra, real estate agent at LPT Realty in Leander, TX.

Put simply, the Lone Star State doesn’t force you to sacrifice space, amenities, or lifestyle to find a home within your budget.

“If you’re a veteran looking to establish roots after military service, that flexibility can make a meaningful difference,” Guerra explains.

Texas also has a long-standing connection to the military.

“I grew up in San Antonio, proudly known as Military City, USA, home to Joint Base San Antonio, including Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, and Randolph. Now, working in the Austin area, I'm also near Camp Mabry and Fort Hood. Military families are an important part of these communities,” says Guerra.

There’s an established VA healthcare system as well.

“For example, in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, Dallas has a full-service VA hospital.  Fort Worth has a large VA outpatient clinic,” says Elizabeth Lane, real estate agent at HomeSmart Realty in Dallas.

Additionally, Texas offers no state individual income tax, potential property tax exemptions for qualifying disabled veterans, and access to military and veteran support networks.

There's also a strong sense of community and diverse employment opportunities.

“Companies like Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron have a large presence in North Texas and like to recruit veterans,” adds Lane.

Tennessee offers a unique mix of benefits for military homebuyers.

First and foremost, there’s no state income tax.

“On top of that, Tennessee has some of the lowest property taxes in the U.S., ranking roughly eighth to 10th lowest, depending on the specific index,” says Wendy Monday, real estate agent at Broker Onward Real Estate in Nashville, TN.

By contrast, states such as New Jersey and Illinois have significantly higher tax rates, which add considerably to the cost of homeownership.

Also, Nashville is one of the premier healthcare hubs in the country, making top-quality medical care exceptionally accessible locally.

It boasts an incredibly high density of Level 1 Trauma Centers, top-tier children's hospitals, and specialized emergency rooms right in the metro area.

“You won't have to travel to another city or state if you or a family member ever face a complex diagnosis or require a rare medical specialist,” Monday explains.

#5535. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.
